speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (for the Minister of International Trade) moved:
speechtext: That this House supports the negotiation of a bilateral trading arrangement with the United States, as part of the government's multilateral trade policy, while protecting our political sovereignty, social programs, agricultural marketing systems, the auto industry, and our unique cultural identity.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to report to the House on the progress of the
Canada-U.S. trade initiatives. I welcome the opportunity to speak to the House on this matter of historic importance. I, along with the rest of the country, very much look forward to the opinions which will be expressed by the Leaders of the opposition Parties on this very important matter.

Mr. Speaker, today we start a historic debate on initiatives that may make the next century Canada's own.

In this historic debate Members of all Parties will be addressing the motion which you have just set out. This motion is designed to create jobs, to generate new wealth, and to create new economic opportunities in all regions of Canada, particularly those which are presently going through great economic difficulties. Because this trade initiative is part of a comprehensive package designed to improve Canada's competitive position for the 21st century, I tell you with pride that the Government of Canada shall today support the resolution in the House of Commons.
Hear, hear!

The backdrop of this requires a little explanation. The scope of our relationship is worthy of mention itself. There is $200 billion a year in bilateral trade with the United States, over 75 per cent of which is duty free. This is the largest trading arrangement between two countries anywhere in the world. It is an enormous amount which presents enormous opportunities and great difficulties. Thirty per cent of our GNP comes directly from our exports and about 80 per cent of those exports go to the United States. Most importantly, almost 2.5 million Canadian jobs depend directly on the American market, the richest and most dynamic market in the world which is sitting right on our doorstep. This measure is designed on behalf of all people of Canada, from the people who are hurting in Alberta to the people of Newfoundland and the people of the interior of British Columbia who need help. This measure is designed to ensure that those areas of the country get their kick at the can through enhanced bilateral trade.
Hear, hear!

There have been troubling developments in Congress. Over the last number of years the United States has been running a very serious trade deficit. Last year it was in the neighbourhood of $170 billion U.S. Such action sometimes brings out the worst in all of us, including the United States. People get scared. They go back to the reactions of the 1930s and throw up protectionist measures. A wave of protectionism has already meant action against our hogs, our steel, our lumber and our potash. The most important and worrisome part of this, albeit understandable, is that Senators and Congressmen in the United States, seeing the decline of smoke-stack industries and large pockets of unemployment develop in traditional areas of wealth, take these measures.
March 16, 1987

They are looking for what they consider to be the unfair traders. However, one of the major problems upon which I invite the House to reflect is that Canada is a fair trader. We are not an unfair trader seeking unfair access to anybody else's market. As Congress prepares to initiate this competitive legislation, which is trade legislation, the United States is saying that if we want to do business in their markets, this is the price of poker in reference to people they consider to be unfair traders and whom they name regularly. Canada is a fair trader. We do not want to be caught up in a net designed for the unfair seeking access to the American market. We have a history of fair trading and a history of generating prosperity through fair trade. This is designed to strike a fair deal with the United States.
Hear, hear!

The trends in trade are there for all to see. They are toward blocks. Japan's emergence as a superpower in trade after the war brought about, in some measure, the creation of the European Economic Community which is now a group of 320 million people within which trade is free, economic intercourse is of the highest and most significant order, and growth and prosperity come about because of the dropping of those barriers.
In another area of the world and for other reasons, but with the fundamentals still in place, Australia and New Zealand have sought and obtained a free trade arrangement between themselves. They are far away from the United States and Europe, yet the structures and objectives apply to them. Over the weekend and today the ASEAN nations from Singapore to the Philippines have been looking at structures which would give them a new free trade association involving hundreds of millions of people. In light of these developments, our domestic market of 25 million people begins to look small and vulnerable. What are our trading options when we strip away the rhetoric? What options are available to any industrialized country? There is GATT, there are sectoral initiatives and there is the possibility of a comprehensive bilateral trade arrangement.
We have been members of GATT for 40 years. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) led a major delegation at Punta del Este where we reaffirmed our commitment to the multilateral trading process. However, specific problems exist in the United States. Steel is very much next on the American agenda, and I see Members here from the Burlington area who are in charge of the steel caucus. The GATT process takes time. The Tokyo round took six years to negotiate and eight years to implement. We cannot wait that long.
Hear, hear!

The sectoral initiatives attempted by the previous Government have failed because of the new climate
Bilateral Trade
that exists in the United States. Those initiatives are not good enough.
There is one initiative that is not exclusive from the GATT but very much complementary of our GATT international exercise. It is a comprehensive bilateral agreement with the United States under Section 24 of the GATT which will put Canada and the United States at the forefront of liberalized trade here and around the world.

And why are we conducting both bilateral and multilateral negotiations, Mr. Speaker? When we decided to engage officially in trade negotiations with the United States, we knew this would be controversial, that all the old bug bears would be resurrected and that it would fan the flames of past partisan debate on the subject. We have decided to go ahead, regardless of the political risk, because we felt it was in the national interest. Why? Simply because without economic prosperity, there can be no cultural and social development in Canada, and to provide for prosperity, we must preserve and expand our export markets.
Canadians export to many countries in the world, but our main market, and in fact the wealthiest and biggest market on this planet is the United States, our next door neighbour. The jobs of several million Canadians depend on it, but access for our goods and services to the U.S. market, as to any other market, is being increasingly threatened by the wave of protectionism and the undue recourse to legislation that presently predominates in international trade.
There are examples of how this affects every province. I am thinking of Quebec, where annual exports total $22 billion, of which $17 billion worth goes to the United States. There are hundreds of thousands of jobs in Quebec that depend directly on the secure U.S. market. Fifteen billion dollars worth of Quebec exports go directly to the United States, and that is to the United States alone! Fifteen billion is what it cost to build the James Bay project, the project of the century. That is how important the U.S. market is to Quebec. It means that Quebec's annual exports to the United States equal the total cost of the James Bay project, and we know the tremendous impact that particular project had on expanding Quebec's economy. And that is why we want to do this. We want to minimize the risks and maximize the benefits. We want to create jobs and boost the economy through our trade initiatives, whether it is in Quebec, in British Columbia or in any other region in Canada.

Our over-all objective is clear-cut. It is to try to carve out a unique trading relationship with the United States of America that will create jobs, end trade harassment, introduce stability, eliminate trade barriers, enhance competitiveness, spur productivity and build an instrument of liberalized trade between the two greatest trading partners in the world. It will be an agreement that can serve as a model for all countries

March 16, 1987
Bilateral Trade
seeking relief from protectionism, growth in the Third World, and more liberalized access to markets everywhere.
This is not a selfish initiative but it has clear advantages to both sides. We hope it will eventually be seen as a signal against the kinds of vulgar and selfish measures of protectionism and be seen as a noble example of generosity and growth. We can show all developing countries in the world that it is not an initiative of protectionism or cutting off our markets but one by which markets can grow and we can accept more and more goods from Third World countries so that we genuinely contribute through trade to building a better and more equitable world.
Hear, hear!

Our highest priority is to have an agreement that ends the threat to Canadian industry from U.S. protectionists who harass and restrict our exports through the misuse of trade remedy laws. Let me leave no doubt that first, a new regime on trade remedy laws must be part of the agreement. Second, because trading is so clearly a two-way street, our negotiators have been instructed to ensure that the elimination of existing tariffs takes place gradually, with adequate transition arrangements that are sensitive to the needs of Canadian industry and Canadian workers. Third, it is clear that non-tariff barriers increasingly distort trade. Our negotiators have, therefore, been instructed to negotiate a broad and comprehensive agreement addressing these issues, including changes to government procurement practices. For example, if Canada were to capture 1 per cent of the government procurement market in North America, it could result in the creation of 75,000 new jobs in this country.
Let me turn to the area of agriculture. Our goal is straightforward. It is to help Canadian farmers by increasing the predictability and security of access of exports by the farm sector through ending the deeply destructive subsidization of exports while preserving our farm support policies and the operation of our marketing boards at the same time. These are the principal Canadian objectives.
If the United States wants to increase access to our market and truly wants Canada to sign precedent-setting agreements that could indeed serve as a great model for the world, then our desires must be respected and our wishes accommodated. Otherwise, there will be no deal.
However, we recognize that a good deal must be one that is fair to both sides. We make it very clear that we do not approach our commercial relationships with the United States as an enemy. The United States is a sovereign, hard-nosed nation with its own national interests to protect. It confronts Canada in the same situation, as a sovereign powerful nation with our own interests to protect, as we shall. We recognize that the deal cannot favour only one side. If such an agreement is to have any durability and value, or have any significance as a model in the world, it must be a fair deal. There must be growth and prosperity in the United States as well as in
Canada so that both sides to this agreement shall prosper to the ultimate benefit of the entire world.

So, given these circumstances, if that is the objective, what was our approach, Mr. Speaker? I think the approach was coherent. First, clear declarations of intentions; second, an exhaustive preparation of the case; and third, a historic degree of consultations and co-operation with the provinces, the industry and, we tried, the labour movement.
First, Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) tabled his document entitled A New Direction for Canada in November 1984, he stated that if we want to promote expansion through export trade we must gain easier and more reliable access to foreign markets under the best conditions possible.
Second, the January 1985 green paper How to Secure and Enhance Canadian Access to Export Markets clearly defined the challenge. It stated: With respect to trade policy, attention focuses on-and on the possibility of taking fresh approaches in the conduct of Canada-U.S. trade relations. Then in the month of March, two years ago tomorrow, I met with President Reagan in Quebec City and we reached agreement on our objective to create a safer climate for bilateral trade and reinforce the multilateral trade system. This initiative was followed by a statement I had the honour to make before the House on September 26, 1985 when I said this: Economics, geography, common sense and the national interest dictate that we try to secure and expand our trade with our closest and largest trading partner. Then there was the external trade advisory committee made up of representatives of all levels of Canadian society under the distinguished chairmanship of Walter Light, various groups of sectorial consultation on external trade.
Fifteen advisory groups, representing all areas of the Canadian economy, from our farms to our steel products to our apparel industry, to mining, to goods and services, were formed. Three hundred or so people, men and women from the best parts of our private sector, came together in intimate consultation with the Government over a period of 18 months in order to help prepare us for these negotiations and to work with us, as they continue to do today.
At the First Ministers' Conference in Halifax we set out the beginning of the process where the Government would consult with the First Ministers on a regular basis. That, too, was a very important indication of our preparation and consultation and our desire to obtain a deal which is good for all Canada. Then there was the vote in the American Senate which gave the green light to its participation in May of 1986. We needed that, of course, because it was at that point in time that the forces of negotiation could effectively be engaged.
March 16, 1987



As to federal-provincial consultations, there were 14 federal-provincial meetings of Ministers and senior officials-an unprecedented series of events, Mr. Speaker. I also had four meetings with the provincial premiers on the question of trade negotiations with the United States, and two more meetings are slated for June and September. This is a first in Canadian history.

This is historic co-operation in terms of the manner in which we wanted it to proceed. Twenty-two years ago, to put it in some contrast, the Government of Canada sent down a group of negotiators to conclude the Auto Pact with the United States of America. They did the Auto Pact and they did a good deal. However, they did it without so much as a by your leave to the duly elected Government of Ontario at the time. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, federal-provincial relations have clearly changed, and very much for the better.
I want to indicate the extent to which this preparation and, I think, this thoughtful consultation with all areas of national life nevertheless had to come together at one bargaining position. While we wanted very much to co-operate with the provinces, and we have, and I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I have said very clearly to the First Ministers, and I say very clearly to the House, the responsibility for international treaty making lies with the federal Government and the Parliament of Canada and it shall not be diluted under any circumstances, we proceeded to select in our judgment the very best team, headed by the very best international and commercial negotiator. I had the honour of asking for, and receiving, the acceptance of Ambassador Simon Reisman who was present on behalf of Canada at the creation of the GATT and who has worked all his life in the Public Service up to the position of Deputy Minister of Finance. Under the instructions of previous governments, he very successfully negotiated the Auto Pact, which has brought such benefits to Canada, notwithstanding predictions to the contrary from other people in this House that it was not going to work. You will hear them again today. The Auto Pact worked because Simon Reisman was the best negotiator in Canada, and we brought him on side to do that job again for the country.
I suppose this leads us to one of the key questions, the rationale and reasoning: why did the Government undertake this historic initiative? It is risky. It provokes controversy and sometimes vexatious and silly questions. It is a "when did you stop beating your wife" situation until you produce the results. We knew that. My Government introduced this historic initiative to create jobs and ensure economic equality for all regions of Canada. Since September of 1984, job creation in Canada has surpassed that of any other industrialized country. We have created 705,000 new jobs as of Friday of last week. Our national unemployment figures have gone from 11.7 per cent down to 9.6 per cent in two years. That is not bad at all.
Bilateral Trade
However, Mr. Speaker, if you look at Friday's figures, I think therein you will see the tragedy. Look at the imbalances in Friday's latest unemployment statistics. These imbalances are largely reflected in our regions and the geography of Canada. Unemployment is down to 9.6 per cent nationally, but in Newfoundland and Labrador unemployment is at 18.4 per cent, and at the other extremity of the country, in British Columbia, unemployment is at 13.3 per cent. Yet in the industrialized heartland of Canada, in Ontario, unemployment is down to 6.8 per cent and in Manitoba it is down to 6.7 per cent, the lowest in the land. What these figures tell us is that over a period of decades, inadvertently, but because of our history and our trading patterns, we are in the process of building two Canadas, one which is rich and promising and one which is underdeveloped and underemployed. That is unacceptable because this Party and this Government stand for one Canada, fairness and equality of opportunity for all.
This is a vital part of that process which will ensure equality of opportunity to all Canadians whoever they are, wherever they live and whatever they do. We are delighted with the prosperity in Manitoba, in Ontario and in certain other regions of the country, but we cannot build prosperity and genuine growth in the country by diminishing anyone else's wealth. What we want is to ensure that Newfoundlanders, British Columbians, Albertans, and others, get their chance, too. They must be given the opportunity to trade their way to new prosperity. That is why I call upon all Hon. Members of the House to set aside the shibboleths and to tell Canadians exactly where they stand today. Are they for this growth and prosperity or are they clinging to the past, because today is a day for the future.
What are the obstacles we have considered? Clearly, in something this important there have been and will continue to be obstacles. First, there is the fact that there are no guarantees. Premier Bourassa of Quebec said that this was a risky but indispensable move, that it had to be done, because the market of 25 million is no longer sufficient in the 21st century to guarantee the kinds of jobs we need. Notwithstanding the progress we have made, and no one can dispute the creation of the 705,000 new jobs, there are still 1.2 million unemployed. It is because I am interested in this, and my Government is interested in this, notwithstanding the risks and not because of the difficulties-we know there are difficulties-we know this requires leadership and daring. There are 1.2 million people still unemployed who are looking to the Parliament of Canada for leadership. I am telling those people that there are new opportunities. Hundreds of thousands of new jobs can be created through trade. This motion is a motion of hope and belief in Canada. That is why I ask the leadership of all Parties to set aside partisanship and to say yes to a more prosperous Canada.

Hear, hear!

March 16, 1987
Bilateral Trade

There are legitimate concerns that have been raised at various times-entirely legitimate concerns. I tried as best I could to deal with some of them in the House when I indicated that the negotiations would not affect our political sovereignty, our system of social programs, our commitment to fight regional disparities, our commitment to defend our unique cultural identity, or our special linguistic character. These make up the essence of Canada. They are not at issue in these negotiations. They are legitimate concerns that we have tried as best we can to deal with in the type of atmosphere of fear and panic that some people try to promulgate. We will try to deal with them on a continuing basis.
I wish to salute the leadership and maturity of the Premiers who have set aside the attractiveness of these ephemeral techniques to deal with some of the fundamental issues which have ensured that the profile of a major trading arrangement deal is now emerging. There is indifference in the United States. There has been historic indifference in the United States which has been overcome in large measure-
Oh, oh!

We will get to the Liberals in a minute. The whole country is waiting to hear their position. I think the Liberals should have the courtesy of allowing others to set out theirs. They may disagree with the position of the Government, but they have to acknowledge that we have one position, not two, three or four.
Hear, hear!

Canadian issues were on the back burner in the United States, something which we have managed to overcome. We have done this through initiatives with President Reagan. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has had quarterly meetings with Secretary Shultz. There have been meetings with Secretary Baker, as well as our visit in Canada with Senator Bensten and the leadership that he is seeking to provide to the Senate Finance Committee. We have dealt with the serious question, and let us acknowledge it, of historic indifference in the United States to many of our Canadian concerns. The matter has now been taken from the back burner to a point at which the President of the United States in his State of the Union Address indicated his commitment to bring about a free trade arrangement with Canada. That indicates that we have begun to make some serious progress.
Then, of course, in terms of obstacles, I will acknowledge that in a parliamentary system one of the problems has been the confusion in the Opposition. The signals that go out to the financial community, the signals that go out to the world, the signals that go out to the various negotiators causes the Americans to wonder where the Official Opposition stands. As 1 have been able to understand it so far, the Liberal policy has to be with respect to trying to garner support on both sides of the issue, unless the issue is particularly sensitive, in which case the Leader of the Liberal Party does not show up to vote.
With respect to the Liberal Party, I can say it no better than Donald Macdonald, a distinguished colleague of my right hon. friend, said it, as reported in The Toronto Star. He said that in a bizarre turn of events Liberal delegates passed a resolution backing free trade in the morning, then supported a policy opposed to free trade at the day's end. Donald Macdonald called the stand of the Party incoherent. Macdonald, who headed a royal commission into the economy last year that favoured free trade, noted that the Party voted for multilateral negotiations, bilateral negotiations, and sectoral negotiations. "From the outside, we look pretty stupid," said Mr. Macdonald. In the national interest I call upon the Leader of the Opposition to deal with that stupidity today and to put the Liberal Party clearly on the record in support of a great national initiative.
Hear, hear

With regard to the NDP, we have the resolution of yesterday's convention to consider. As I understand it, the resolution calls upon Canada to withdraw from the comprehensive negotiations with the United States.
Shame, shame!

We have the Leader of the NDP saying that he will propose a policy of full employment. When he is asked how he will do it he does not have the foggiest idea. We know now that it will not be by trade. I tell the Leader of the NDP and the apostles of reaction who have taken over a few of the positions of leadership of the CLC this. Do not become hostages to the past. Reject this call for protectionism because jobs for ordinary Canadians come from trade. We need your help in supporting this kind of great national enterprise.
Hear, hear!

I would now like to deal with the question of research. People say that these matters, of course, have to be considered. Some years ago The Globe and Mail reported that it is often alleged that those supporting liberalized trade have not done their homework. In reality, that is far more true of those who oppose free trade. Among the critics, therefore, rhetoric, passion and a model of nationalism sometimes fill the gap or conceal a defence of economic privilege.
The article went on to ask who the real nationalists are in the free trade debate and who are the defenders of special interests. Who has done the research and who appeals to generalized fears? Those seem to me to be legitimate questions for this House to consider.
The Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston), presumably speaking on behalf of his Party, said that the point is that those who argue that a free trade agreement will cost jobs must also look at the other side of the coin. What will protectionism cost us? What will the absence of a free trade arrangement cost us? I salute the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount for his vision.
March 16, 1987
Hear, hear!

Then there is the MacDonald Commission to consider, as well as the Economic Council of Canada, the C. D. Howe Institute and the Institute for International Economics. Anyone who will contest this-and it is a free country, please go ahead since now is the time to do it-let us hear from you. Let us hear from the research. Let us hear from the scientific data that is available. All of the research, all of the hard practical evidence shows beyond a shadow of a doubt that eliminating trade barriers makes us better off individually and nationally. It makes us richer, gives us more, and permanent jobs and a better future. That is what all of the research indicates. There has been no question of that so far.
What did the Macdonald Commission say? This was a commission headed by a former Minister of Finance, a very distinguished member of the Liberal Party, along with a group of colleagues and millions of dollars-I think $20 million was spent on research. The best people in Canada looked at this issue for a number of years. They concluded, on a prudent course, that free trade will help to make us richer, and by making us richer it will strengthen the fabric of our country and increase our self-confidence.

One of the members of the Macdonald royal inquiry commission, who signed the report after three or four years of inquiry and studies, was Montreal lawyer Michel Robert who has since become President of the Liberal Federation of Canada. I would now expect Mr. Robert to maintain his support for free trade as he did in the signed report, the Macdonald report.
The Economic Council of Canada said that Canada can go forward with these arrangements:
-or it can go backward, accepting the steady erosion of our current access to export markets created by protectionist trade actions.
The Economic Council of Canada forecast a possible-over and above what this Government is going to be able to do with foreign investment and with increased productivity-370,000 new jobs as a result of the initiative if the productivity is increased by, as it indicates, a conservative 5 per cent in certain areas. There will be 370,000 new jobs, Mr. Speaker. Can you imagine what this will do for Nova Scotia, and the help it will give to New Brunswick, Newfoundland and the interior of British Columbia? These are hard facts put out by a distinguished group of economists, Canada's leading group of economists. They say there are hundreds of thousands of new jobs. If Hon. Members are opposed to it, let them give us the information that justifies their absence of faith in Canada.
Hear, hear!

Richard Lipsey and Murray Smith say that the free trade agreement:
Bilateral Trade
-offers the most promising opportunity to create a more efficient, adaptive, and outward-looking Canadian-and U.S.-economy that would provide rising living standards and expanding employment opportunities for the great majority of people.
The Business Council of British Columbia said:
-we must adopt long-term policies based on economic realities which recognize our relationship with the U.S.

La Presse: "Mr. Mulroney's statement is realistic, opens the door to a wide-ranging agreement with the United States and respects the right of Canadians to define the content of a future agreement as negotiations progress". "Canadian culture will never flourish if it fails to stand up to straightforward competition on its own turf, and it must do so outside the country as well."

John Kenneth Galbraith said:
I read in the papers that Canadians are concerned that free trade will impair their sovereignty and bring Canada ever more dangerously under American influence. This is nonsense. The American influence is there, no one can doubt, but it is a factor of geography, not of trade.
That is why I ask Hon. Members to set aside the nonsense and to deal with trade as a job creating issue for Canada.
Hear, hear!

Pierre Lortie, President of Provigo, one of our great businessmen and economic thinkers in Quebec, says: "It would be criminal not to pursue aggressively negotiations for an agreement with the United States".

The Canada West Foundation said:
The second compelling reason for arguing for a free trade arrangement with the U.S. is the competitiveness issue, what we like to call the faith in Canadians approach. This approach argues that by adopting a more open market and competitive spirit in Canada an environment will be created which would raise Canadian living standards, employment prospects and quality of life.
The Atlantic Provinces Chamber of Commerce say that this trade is:
to promote industrial decentralization in Canada-
Surely, Mr. Speaker, in light of the unemployment results, notwithstanding tremendous progress by this House and this country in the last two and a half years, and we hear the plea of the Atlantic Provinces Chamber of Commerce and the plea that Premier Peckford made at the First Ministers, Conference where he indicated that Newfoundlanders since coming into confederation had only about 52 or 53 per cent per capita income of people in Ontario who are now at 115 per cent as opposed to 52 per cent, this is the growing of two Canadas, and it is unacceptable. We must require and have the assistance of everyone, including the Opposition Parties for people in other parts of Canada who need jobs and prosperity, and trade is the way you guarantee that.

March 16, 1987
Bilateral Trade
In southwestern Ontario, in London, there is a very generous view of the Canadian responsibility. We read:
The better and safer bet would be to try to negotiate a freer trade agreement with the U.S. that would open up new opportunities for productive Canadian firms and businesses, while also safeguarding social, cultural and political values essential to our Canadian identity.
The Saskatoon Star-Phoenix wrote:
To be too fearful of possible consequences would be to invite greater economic isolation.
Perhaps I could conclude-
Tell us something.
When do you start your speech?
I will be glad to quote from a great Canadian nationalist, Richard Gwyn, whose credentials are unchallenged.
Oh, oh!

The Liberals and the New Democrats are laughing at a journalist of the esteem and commitment to Canada of a Richard Gwyn. I tell Hon. Members his credentials are unchallenged. I will read a statement from his book:
A national vote in favour of bilateral free trade would represent the ultimate declaration by Canadians of self-confidence in themselves, confidence both in their ability to compete and in their ability to continue as a distinct political and social unit.
There is a commitment to Canada, Mr. Speaker.
Hear, hear!

We have garnered the support in this initiative, although some parties would suggest that we have been alone. We have not been alone. The Premiers, the Governments of all political stripes, business leaders from John Bulloch to Jean de Grandpre, from Tom D'Aquino to Pierre Lorti, from Pierre Macdonald to Jacques Parizeau are with us. It is important to note as we begin the debate the extent to which those outside of this House are non-partisan, the extent to which people do take a broader view of politics, politicians and the future of our country.

The Canadian Chamber of Commerce has expressed its support, and also the Canadian Federation of Independent Businesses, the Consumers Association of Canada, the Canadian Export Association, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, and the Business Council on National Issues.

Negotiators for both countries should strive for the largest possible elimination of barriers to trade, having a broad comprehensive free trade agreement in mind. Such an approach would be in the best interest of both countries.
That is the statement from the Hon. Marc Lalonde.
Oh, oh!
Is this where you are getting your advice?
He is the guy who designed the National Energy Program.

And what are the results, Mr. Speaker?
As far as we are concerned, we know there is no magic formula. The process is always a painful one in a country like ours, especially in the case of such important and historical initiatives. Nevertheless, to me and my colleagues, international trade stands for jobs, prosperity, regional growth and a future for our children. Mr. Speaker, we must consider the impact that initiatives such as establishing new trade relations with the United States will have by strengthening the economy and the unity of this country in the next century.

Nothing is perfect, we acknowledge. Let us consider at the end of the day the alternatives. Who knows, maybe there will be strokes of brilliance and we look forward to hearing them. We will listen to them dispassionately and carefully. If the Liberal Party or the New Democratic Party has a progressive, dynamic suggestion in terms of the manner in which we create new jobs-there is no pride of fraternity in something as important as unemployment-we will take the idea, consider it in the House and, if it will create those kinds of jobs, we will deal with it appropriately.
But consider the implications for Canada for economic growth and Canadian unity of new trading arrangements with our largest partner which can produce hundreds of thousands of new jobs, which can increase our productivity, spur on our competitiveness here and around the world. Consider that in the light as well of what has already been initiated with the provinces, the Government of Ontario and all the other provinces, of a new commitment to national science and technology programs. Consider that in the light as well of another building block, so important for all Members of this House, namely, a question of tax reform based on fairness and equity bound together by a new constitutional formula which will allow Quebec to be brought back into the Canadian family. This is a building block of greatness. This is what the House is considering today as the future of Canada. It is an act of faith in Canada.
It has often been said that young men have visions and old men dream dreams. This is a day for Canada. This is a day both for visions and great dreams. It is a commitment to the future of Canada. It is a commitment to the youth of Canada, to our unity and to our integrity as a nation.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate should have been held two years ago today, the day before the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) met the President of the United States at the so-called Shamrock Summit and committed our two countries by way of a joint
March 16, 1987

declaration on trade. That declaration was made and jointly signed by the head of our Government and the President of the United States without any prior parliamentary debate, without any prior warning to the Parliament and people of Canada, and without any mandate from the people of Canada because it was not an issue in the last general election.
My first observation this afternoon is to say that despite the opportunity given to us by the Government for the debate, after listening to the Prime Minister this morning and into the afternoon, Canadians are no further ahead and are no wiser than we were two years ago. We wonder why we had this debate.
Hear, hear!

It is true, we have learned, that the Prime Minister has a great clipping service. He called from among newspapers and reports of Chambers of Commerce which he could find for some selective approval. He cited my good friend and successor in the Ministry of Finance, Donald Macdonald. I said to Donald, when he came out with the report of the Macdonald Commission and asked Canadians to take a "leap of faith": "Fine, take a leap of faith, but as a Canadian before I do that I would prefer to know where 1 land".
The Prime Minister has given us no details, no further information, no further factual data, and no precision at all on the Government's position in the negotiations with the United States. We do not know what is negotiable. We do not know what is not negotiable.
We read the motion. It has been called a motherhood motion. We would have thought the Prime Minister might have given us more explanation of what the Government meant. He did not talk much about sovereignty and how we would reconcile that sovereignty in a comprehensive free trade arrangement with the United States. He mentioned nothing about our social programs, how they were to be interfaced. He did not make a defence of our agricultural marketing systems, as the motion sets forth. He made absolutely no reference to the auto industry or to the Auto Pact, more specifically. He talked in only vague terms once again about our unique cultural identity. Canadians are no further ahead after listening to the Prime Minister through their representatives in Parliament, than they were two years ago tomorrow when he made that declaration with the President of the United States.
Of course it is quite clear now that the Government continues to adhere to its game plan as outlined in the leaked communications strategy document which we produced in the House of Commons a year and a half ago. When the issue of free trade was first brought to the attention of Canadians, the game plan as declared in that document-and its authenticity has never been denied-quite simply was to keep Canadians ignorant of what was being discussed in the trade negotiations because the less Canadians knew, the better chance the Government would have to sell it.
Bilateral Trade
The document, if I might recall, also recommended a dirty tricks campaign against those perceived Members of Parliament who might take issue with the initiative of the Government, including a number of Members of Parliament who sit on this side of the House, beginning with the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra. It is a strategy on how to get us in our own particular ridings if we opposed the initiative of the Government of Canada. I quote from that document:
The strategy should rely less on educating the general public than on getting the message that the trade initiative is a good idea; in other words, a selling job.
Those were the words of that communique. That has been, and consistently so, the strategy of the Government. It was maintained today in the Prime Minister's speech, because we do not know any more than we did two years ago about where the Government stands in these negotiations on the major issues which have to be dealt with in the negotiations.
A year and a half ago when a resolution was introduced in the House we had a vague 15-minute speech from the Prime Minister clothed in generalities, clothed in shibboleth, laced with rhetoric, and garnished with his usual hyperbole. We got that again today; it took him a little longer. When we are able to analyse and compare the two speeches, he was probably more forthcoming in that first 15-minute speech a year and a half ago.
Perhaps the Opposition should not have pressed so hard for the Government to bring the matter before Parliament or prevailed upon the Government to come clean with Canadians, to let us know, as representatives of people from one end of Canada to the other, where the Government is taking us, what are the general parameters, what is at stake, what is not at stake, what is at issue, and what is not at issue. Perhaps we should not have pressed so hard because the Prime Minister has been a great disappointment to the country this morning.
I thought we were to have a statesmen-like review. For a while the Prime Minister restrained himself, and then of course he descended into the style of the bear pit that he likes. 1 will try to resist but, since he has opened the door, I think Members of Parliament on this side of the House will be excused if from time to time we do not retain the same shrewd control of ourselves that we should.
[ Translation]
Concluding a free trade agreement would bring about profound changes in nearly all aspects of our economy in the years to come. It would have a considerable impact on our way of life, our trading habits, our national sovereignty, our independence and certainly on the quality of life in the northern part of this continent.
The Prime Minister has embarked upon a risky undertaking, and he is once again refusing to let us know the stakes involved. The Government has no mandate from Canadians to negotiate a free trade agreement. There was no mention of this during the election campaign, and in fact we would not even be discussing the matter here in the House, if the opposition Parties had not insisted on having this debate.

March 16, 1987
Bilateral Trade
Mr. Speaker, I also think that the presentation of this motion at this point in time relates much more to the domestic problems now experienced by the Government than to our trade relations with the United States.

This debate should have happened first, not last. As the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on Canada's International Relations stated in 1985, and I should like to quote from the unanimous report:
It is premature for Canada to initiate formal bilateral negotiations with the United States to determine the receptivity to liberalizing bilateral trade. After a ministerial report to Parliament on the outcome of these discussions and on whether certain conditions have been met, the Government should decide whether the prospects are sufficiently promising to continue on to detailed negotiations.
What the joint report suggested in unanimous terms is that Parliament ought to be apprised in general terms of the discussions. There ought to be a consensus on the parameters as to how those discussions ought to be directed and how they should go, and only then should formal negotiations be initiated with the United States. The Government of our country ignored that advice. Instead, it went headlong into a process for which it was ill-prepared.

What I had asked at the time, and what my colleagues on this side of the House and the committee members have since asked on many occasions, was that Parliament and the Canadian people be made fully aware of all the parameters of Canada's position before the beginning of official negotiations with the United States.
We have asked on several occasions in committee and elsewhere for the cost-benefit analysis of the impact of such a deal upon Canada. In May, 1986, the Government released 24 trade-enhancement studies, but every piece of information which would have given us the slightest indication of the impact on a given sector or a given region of Canada was censored. Whole pages of those documents were absolutely eliminated. What was missing in the 18-minute gap in the Watergate tape is just a tiny blip compared to what was left out of these documents.
The Government was sticking to its game plan, an approach popularized by the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) who said during the last election campaign: "If we told you what we were going to do, we'd never get elected". I think that was the most honest, forthcoming and frank statement we have ever heard from a member of the government side.
Hear, hear!

Canadians are giving a clear message to the Prime Minister. They are saying: "Mr. Prime Minister, would you deal honestly with us, would you give us the facts, would you give us the data upon which we can make judgments about the affairs of state and the issues before us?" I believe that if given the facts and if given an opportunity to assess those facts over a reasonable period of time, Canadians will make the right judgment. The gap in the process now before the country is that the Government does not trust Canadians, it is not giving Canadians the facts and it is not allowing the people of Canada to make a fair judgment about what is going on.
After this morning's intervention by the Prime Minister, we still do not know what is being negotiated. The vocabulary changes almost as often as the Prime Minister's valet changes his shirt. I remind the Prime Minister of the statement he made in 1983 on free trade. He said during the leadership campaign of June 1983 in a debate with the now Minister of Transport and the now Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) about free trade: "It affects Canadian sovereignty and we will have none of it". Then on July 4, 1985, The Ottawa Citizen quoted the Prime Minister as saying: "We never discussed free trade. Enhanced trade or trade agreements impact not only on the United States but on our trading relationship with allies and upon GATT".
A little later on July 8, 1985,-

Brian Mulroney, quoted in a Montreal daily, Le Devoir, said: "I agree with the expression "improvement of trade relations" but not with the words "free trade."

These were the opinions upon which the people of Canada were entitled to rely. These were the opinions upon which the Parliament of Canada was entitled to rely before, suddenly, the Prime Minister, in order to enhance his photo image with the President, unrehearsed and unplanned, with no advice to the people of Canada, signed that joint declaration.
Canadians want to know how far we are going and in what direction. Is it free trade? Is it freer trade? Is it enhanced trade or is it a bilateral arrangement? Is it a comprehensive free trade arrangement? The motion before the House does not answer those questions. Just three hours prior to the motion being printed, the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) in response to questions in the House of Commons last Wednesday called it a comprehensive free trade arrangement. At the same time, in response to another question, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) called it a comprehensive trade arrangement. Yesterday in her CTV interview, the Minister simply called it free trade. In fact, she used the words "free trade" 14 times in that single interview. What is it?
What we have before us today is not a free trade motion. It is either a considerable retreat from the Government's position as expressed in the joint declaration, as expressed in Ministerial statements and Ministerial responses in the House of Commons and as expressed to journalists, or it is a disguise to
March 16, 1987

get a comprehensive free trade deal. There is nothing in the motion and there was nothing in the Prime Minister's speech today to tell us which direction the Government really contemplates and where it stands on the issue.

The motion is empty, Mr. Speaker. The motion does not give the House any indication of the direction the Government will take in the negotiations with the United States.
And what about the role of the provinces? There is no consensus among the provincial premiers concerning the nature of the agreement which should be concluded.
Yet, a number of questions under study are related to provincial jurisdiction. They affect provincial purchasing policies: Ontario and Saskatchewan purchase programs, grants to agriculture and industry, and so on.
Last month the Premier of Quebec reiterated his conviction that his province has a right of veto in these negotiations. And the Premier of Ontario expressed the same views.
In their meeting with the Prime Minister last week, eight provincial premiers insisted on the need to ratify any trade agreement Ottawa might sign.
Sad to say, the position of the provincial premiers is the same as ours as members and the same as that of most Canadians: we do not know what the Government is negotiating and, quite simply, we are not confident that it can negotiate an agreement favourable to Canada.

Of course the United States is our largest and most important trading partner. In no way do I contest the emphasis the Prime Minister puts on those figures. Of course we should seek greater access to American markets as part of our over-all opening to the world. However, entering into these talks has been ill-timed. There is rising protectionist sentiments in the United States reflected in the newly elected Democratic Congress. There have been years of trade surpluses with the United States and we felt at the outset that this was not the best time to try to obtain a better over-all deal with the United States.
I would say quite frankly that the Government has been absolutely naive in thinking that the very fact of initiating negotiations with the United States, negotiations on free trade or on whatever, as the motion does not indicate what it is, would by itself dissipate the protectionist sentiment in the United States Congress. Of course that has not happened. During these negotiations we have been held hostage by the Congress and the administration of the United States. At the same time as the Americans were negotiating with our negotiators, presumably for a free trade deal, they imposed a 35 per cent tariff on B.C. shakes and shingles. They forced us to impose on ourselves a 15 per cent export tax on lumber. They forced us to truncate our pharmaceutical legislation in order to please the pharmaceutical companies in the United States. On issue after issue, this country has been held hostage
Bilateral Trade
by the protectionist sentiment in the United States and the very fact of these negotiations has had no influence at all on the conduct or reaction of the Americans.
I think there is a question which needs to be put to the Government, with which the Government has not dealt, and we have put the question to Ministers and to the Prime Minister on other occasions. What is the real purpose of these negotiations on the American side? Reading the recently introduced amendments to the U.S. trade legislation, and particularly that piece of legislation now supported in a Democratic Senate by 53 or 54 Senators on both sides of the aisle, one observes that that legislation does not talk about free trade, freer trade or even fair trade. It is a piece of legislation designed to manage the trade of the United States in the interests of the United States. It sets forth a mechanism making it impossible if fully applied for any country trading with the United States to do so on a bilateral basis. It must do so only subject to the will and whim of the United States Congress.
I ask the Prime Minister if we have an undertaking. What is the real purpose of the Americans? Do they want a free trade arrangement with Canada or are they using this mechanism as a way of extracting from us a series of managed trade agreements to their favour? First lumber; what is next, potash, oil and gas, steel, services? We do not know. We have received no report from the Prime Minister. Surely he told the Premiers where he stood. Surely he told the Premiers what the chances were and what was at stake. If he did, fine, but he certainly has not put Members of Parliament in the same position. We have the fundamental role and duty of voting on this matter and recommending to our constituents what the attitude of the country ought to be.
We in the Liberal Party have always favoured finding ways with the U.S. of enhancing access to each other's markets. We believe our policy must be developed as part of a global approach to trade and not focus solely on the U.S. The Prime Minister says he is impatient with the GATT process, it takes too long. That process has served this country well, because as we cut deals in GATT negotiations we have always been able to make on the side a better arrangement with the U.S. than I believe we will ever be able to make head to head in the current negotiations.
The Government refuses to put forward its actual negotiating position. It gives us conflicting reports as to what is actually being negotiated. This resolution tells us nothing. The Prime Minister added nothing upon which we could assess the position of the negotiations. Therefore we will vote against the motion.
The Government and the Minister for International Trade will probably use the excuse that it cannot tell us where the negotiations are because it would impede the negotiations. Surely the Premiers have been given some idea of where the Government is. We have had a series of selective leaks by Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
March 16, 1987
Bilateral Trade
Reisman and others in order to enhance the Government's position every once in a while, hype up the negotiations and titillate the Canadian public. However, when the people of Canada, through their Members of Parliament, ask for the information they are entitled to concerning the range and parameters of the negotiations, the Prime Minister does not tell us, and neither does the Minister for International Trade. Members of Parliament are left completely in the dark and that we cannot accept.
It appears that if these negotiations continue we are going to be faced with some kind of agreement. Whatever it is, the Government will stagger away from the table and cry victory. We have decided to submit an amendment to this House and to the country outlining the basic conditions we believe must be met in any negotiations with the U.S. We have made it detailed and not followed the Government's example of this vacuous motion before the House. These are the principles of our trade policy as it concerns the United States.
I will introduce the amendment at the proper time, at the conclusion of what I have to say, but the conditions we propose include protection of our sovereignty, limiting of U.S. protectionist action, restoring our previous access on softwood lumber, reduction of non-tariff barriers, preservation of our ability to legislate in areas such as social policy, agriculture, regional development, the environment, financial and service industries, language and culture, the Auto Pact, and the provision of adjustment assistance and the ending of U.S. trade harassment on potash, steel, fish, energy and agriculture. We have set forth a blueprint for the Government, if it continues these negotiations, as to where we stand on the negotiations. We do that because the government motion is far more interesting for what it has excluded than for what it actually says. It is, as The Toronto Star put it, a motherhood resolution. That great newspaper has advised us-
Oh, oh!

-to vote for the resolution, but with due respect to that institution, we would be betraying the people of Canada if we supported the motion, and we do not.
In the motion before the House the Government is simply saying this. Give us a complete and free hand. Trust us. I can assure the Prime Minister that at this time in his mandate the Canadian people do not trust him and we do not trust the future of these negotiations and that is why we are spelling it out in this particular way.
Hear, hear!

Trust us, says the Prime Minister. We will go down and get a good deal. We will do it, the motion says, "while protecting our political sovereignty, social programs, agricultural marketing systems, the auto industry, and our unique cultural identity".
Let us examine that motion because it is a joke, but Canadians are not laughing after hearing the Prime Minister this morning. Are we going to trust that Government to protect our sovereignty? That is the same Government which dithered and delayed over the passage of the Polar Sea through our northern waters. It challenged that passage only after the waters had been traversed by the Polar Sea. Can we trust that Government after it sold out our fishermen to France and our pharmaceutical industry to the U.S? That Government gave away everything the Americans wanted before these negotiations ever began. If you are going to negotiate with the U.S. on any kind of trade, why was FIRA and the National Energy Program dismantled first? Why not leave them as part of the bargaining process? Why throw away all our cards so early? I would enjoy a poker game with the Prime Minister because he lays his cards out before he even knows what is at stake.

Mr. Speaker, are we going to rely on the Government to protect our social programs, this Government which made an attempt to de-index old age security pensions and which, in its three budgets, put an unfair burden on the shoulders of low and middle income Canadians, and widened the gap between rich and poor Canadians as a result of the largest tax increases ever in this country? No, Mr. Speaker, we are not going to put our faith in this Government.

What do the words "agricultural marketing systems" mean? Does it just mean marketing boards or does it include financing through the Farm Credit Corporation? Does it include advance payments for grain under the Canadian Wheat Board Act? Does it include freight rates? We do not know because the motion is deliberately vague, keeping the people of Canada in the dark on the one hand and giving the Government of Canada the widest flexibility on the other. We deserve to know more.
The motion says the Government will protect the auto industry. Does that mean the Auto Pact? The Minister said in her interview, as she has already said 1,001 times, that the Auto Pact is not on the table. However, in the Prime Minister's speech in Montreal last week, although he did not mention it today, he said the Auto Pact was not on the table because the other side had not raised it. However, in the next breath he said if they did raise it, it could become part of the discussions. What is it going to be? If tariffs on auto parts and vehicles are given up, the Auto Pact becomes meaningless.

The motion before the House also affirms that the Government will protect "our unique cultural identity". But what does it mean? Does it include our cultural industries? Where was this protection when the Government authorized the Prentice Hall takeover by the Gulf and Western companies?
March 16, 1987



One of the most glaring omissions from this motion, the rest of it being vague vapidities, is any mention of regional equality and the programs to bring it about. In Montreal and again today the Prime Minister said that the Government would never abandon its commitment to regional development. Why is that not mentioned in the motion? Why is something so fundamental to the governing of this country left out? In those circumstances how can the Prime Minister vote for the motion? How can the Minister of Transport vote for the motion? Indeed, how can any Member on that side of the House vote for the motion? It is a vote, as the Prime Minister said, on Canada's future, but the Government, instead of giving Canadians the facts, is asking this House for a blank cheque.
With regard to the Government's regional economic development policy, the Prime Minister mentioned that the trade option is the one solution for Atlantic Canada. The only trade option that the people of Newfoundland have under this Government is to trade unemployment in Newfoundland for a $4 an hour job in Toronto. The Prime Minister said that we must give Newfoundland, Alberta and B.C. a kick at the can. This morning he gave those provinces a kick in the can. This sounds like the rhetoric of an election speech. During the election campaign he promised to inflict prosperity on Newfoundland. Those were his words. Two years later he is still making the same kind of promise and that promise will not work.

The Prime Minister can say what he likes, but we know the Government's attitude to regional equality. Its spending cut-backs on regional development projects are ample proof of this. The House will recall that spending on these projects dropped from S14 billion in 1984-85 to $12 billion in 1986-87.

In his speech in Montreal before the weekend the Prime Minister said that a trade agreement with the United States "is a critical element for any meaningful regional development strategy". In other words, he is telling the Atlantic, western Canada and northern Canada to wait until we are finished negotiating with the United States, then we will get around to them.

However, seven out of 10 provinces in Canada now have higher unemployment than was the case during the worst days of the recession. For Canadians living in the disadvantaged regions of this country, the Government's message this morning boils down to this: If you don't like it, though, move somewhere else! That is not the Liberal view, Mr. Speaker. We do not want a country where we have to tell Canadians who cannot find jobs in disadvantaged regions: Move to Vancouver, move to Toronto, move to Montreal!
Bilateral Trade

We believe that equality of opportunity is the cornerstone enshrined in the Charter of Rights. No matter where you live you should have an equal opportunity for an education, a job and a secure retirement. That is fundamental to our view of the country. It is constitutionally enshrined but is not recognized in any way in the motion before the House recommending a bilateral arrangement with the United States.
I suspect that these very regional economic development programs are being discussed in the negotiations. 1 suspect that that is why there is no mention of those programs or of regional economic equality in this motion. We have consistently demanded to know what is on the table in these negotiations and what is not on the table. The Government has given us a variety of answers. Sometimes some things are on, sometimes they are off.
Last week the Minister for International Trade told us in the House that we would, in her words, have to find out what is going to be in an over-all agreement before we can identify whether federal or provincial jurisdiction applies. That is incredible. Is she telling the House that she does not know what Mr. Reisman is negotiating, that she does not know what Mr. Reisman and Mr. Murphy are talking about? Is she not informed? If she is informed, why does she not tell us? Why does she not give us some simple responses to some simple questions so that Canadians will have a better inkling of where their Government is taking them?
This motion is so vague that we believe the Government does not really know what it wants. Either it does not know what it wants or it is presuming on the goodwill of the country not to tell us what it wants. Either the Government knows and is not telling, or is in the even more precarious position of not knowing.
The Americans certainly know what they want. The office of the U.S. trade representative, Clayton Yeutter, published a list called the National Trade Estimate; 1986 Report on Foreign Trade Barriers. The top trade representative of the United States has set forth in the Cabinet of the United States a clear list of priorities that he and his Government want to discuss with Canada. I am going to send the Minister a copy so that she will know what the Americans want to discuss even if she is not willing to tell us what Canadians want to discuss. I will put on the record that which the Americans want to discuss because they are very clearly set forth.
They want to discuss all tariffs, especially those on textiles, footwear, paper products, furniture, toys, telecommunications equipment, processed foods, electrical products, railway cars and parts, manufactured metal products, and some auto parts. They want to discuss the elimination of all discriminatory liquor practices; the role of the Canadian Wheat Board, particularly import permits; footwear quotas; standards on plywood; government procurement policies, including Supply and Services' 10 per cent price preference on Canadian content; freight rate subsidies; and copyright protection. They

March 16, 1987
Bilateral Trade
want to discuss pharmaceuticals, especially patent legislation, which, by the way, the Government has already acquiesced to by presenting legislation to increase drug prices for Canadians just to help salvage these trade talks. They want to discuss cross-border broadcasting, magazine advertising, trucking, especially Canada's entry standards; the requirement that data processing of Canadian banks be done in Canada; Investment Canada review of culturally sensitive sectors such as books, films, video and audio recordings; Canadian 50 per cent ownership requirement for oil and gas projects on federal lands; and federal and provincial grants for oil and gas exploration. In addition, they want to discuss financial assistance for oil and gas and mineral exploration, agriculture, publishing, and retail and wholesale commerce; performance requirements on foreign investors; i.e. favouring Canadian suppliers; and postal rates which favour Canadian businesses. That is the American list.
We have had no response from the Government as to where we stand on some of the major items. We have not asked for that type of detail. We know that there must be some negotiating flexibility. However, on the major areas this country should have been as forthcoming as the Americans have been. Whatever one might say about their system, it is an open democracy. The Prime Minister promised us open government and has not given us the type of information we want. Where is our list? What are we after? We do not have the Government's list so have set out our list in our amendment so that the people of Canada will know where the Liberal Party stands on those issues as parameters for the negotiations.
I do not doubt the Prime Minister's word, and I second his feeling, that we are very lucky to be living next to the United States. I think they are a great people. I enjoy, as much as anyone in the House, visiting the United States. We all have American friends and one of three Canadians has an American relative.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for Multiculturalism; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: And there's baseball.

I have a lot of admiration for the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) but he has only been bunting in here. Let us talk about baseball because the Americans always talk about a level playing field. However, they are really referring to a football field. When the Americans talk about fair trade and a level playing field they are talking about a field with their linesmen, their lines, their rules, their ball and their referee. That is the kind of level playing field they are talking about and he ought to remember that.
Hear, hear!

The Americans have the tendency to change the rules when they find they are losing. In the Tokyo Round we gained the right of free access to the American market of Canadian lumber. We paid for that in a trading negotiation. We had to give up other items including computer equipment. When the Americans found that we were
starting to take an appreciable percentage of their domestic market, they changed the rules by using the unilateral countervailing system. The Prime Minister must not be naive in these negotiations. We want meaningful restrictions on countervail.
Speaking of lumber, we saw the Minister's great negotiating skills at work. The U.S. industry called for protection, as it did in 1983. Our lumber industry, supported by good ministerial back-up in 1983, was able to win that case conclusively before the American Inter-Congress Tribunals. The law had not changed since 1983 and the facts had not changed since 1983. Although there was a rising protectionist sentiment in the United States, the main thing that changed was the will and backbone of the Canadian Government to back up a Canadian industry in those negotiations. Undoubtedly, the negotiating prowess of the Minister for International Trade during the lumber dispute will be a case study for business schools across Canada, and presumably even the United States. When is a final offer not a final offer? When is it a final offer? We saw one final offer after another. The Government, through the Minister, pleaded guilty before the American tribunal before the case was ever heard and gave it all the evidence it needed. We still believe that the Minister sold us out and could have done better.
We will wait to see how the issue is eventually determined because the sell-out on Canadian lumber will cost industry at least $600 million per year. If it is ever transferred to a stumpage fee the cost against our industry will probably be $1 billion a year because of the value-added process. Yet the Minister said it is a good deal for Canada and a victory for the country. It will go down as the greatest sell-out in the history of our negotiations with the United States, and the greatest betrayal of a major industry in Canada by a Minister who should be responsible for the export potential of Canada.
The Americans smile because they know it sets a dangerous precedent for other resource and export industries, including pulp and paper, steel, potash, oil and gas, and hydro, as I suggested to the Premier of Quebec.
If this is the style of negotiation we can expect from the Government we will be lucky to keep our shirts on our backs when the matter is eventually brought before the House. That is why the country is nervous and why our Party will not give a blank cheque to the Government. That is why we have asked for more facts and why we are so deeply disappointed with the Prime Minister in failing to use this opportunity for debate to enlarge the factual base upon which Canadians and their Members of Parliament can make a judgment.
I stated from the outset that the Government should have negotiated a standstill agreement on unilateral action, such as harassment to countervail or anti-dumping, prior to the negotiations with the United States. The former Premier of British Columbia, Bill Bennett, took exactly the same position during the lumber dispute. We felt it was illogical for a
March 16, 1987

government of Canada to pursue negotiations in trade with the United States while being beset by unprovoked and unannounced unilateral action. There should not be protectionist harassment if we are supposed to be negotiating a free trade style agreement.
The very day that our negotiators sat down with the Americans, the President of the United States slapped a 35 per cent tariff on British Columbia red cedar shakes and shingles. That was not a good omen for how these negotiations have been carried out. There has not been a good omen since, primarily because of the blanket of secrecy the Government has thrown over the negotiations.
I have also said since the beginning that any agreement with the United States which does not severely limit or eliminate the use of countervail action, such as we saw in the lumber case, will not be worth the paper on which it is written.
The United States has signed a free trade agreement with one other country. It is the State of Israel. In that agreement the Americans did not give up their right to impose countervail action against whatever they consider to be unfair practices. Certainly, members of the Congress tell our Members and leading Senators tell me that the United States Congress is in no mood to give up that remedy under the U.S. Trade Act of 1978. I might point out that in that agreement the United States has the right to prohibit Israel from aiding any new industries. The United States has achieved essentially a controlling element over the future development of that country.
Any deal which allows the current use of countervailing duties will not be fair, will not be free, and will not get the support of Canadians. While we would welcome a dispute resolution mechanism or a joint tribunal between the two countries, an agreement that does not have an appreciable, significant restriction for countervail will not be worth signing on behalf of the country. If there ever is an agreement, under the fast track procedure the Senate, particularly, and perhaps the House of Representatives, will have an opportunity to review whatever document is agreed upon.
The Prime Minister states quite clearly that it is a federal matter, although there will be a need for corresponding provincial legislation in areas of provincial jurisdiction in order for the agreement to be effective. Despite the prerogative of the Government to sign such a treaty without parliamentary approval, I hope the Prime Minister will follow the precedent of the Columbia River Treaty that was signed when Mr. Pearson was Prime Minister. I was Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister concerned at the time and the Government gave Members of Parliament, through a Committee of the House, a full opportunity to examine that treaty, to call the negotiators, as well as the opponents and advocates of the treaty and everyone with a legitimate interest before the parliamentary committee. I hope Members of Parliament, who are elected by the people of Canada, would have a similar right to review the terms and ambit of any agreement with the United States.
Bilateral Trade
In his televised address to the nation last year, the Prime Minister said that our goods would receive "national treatment" in the United States. However, he didn't mention that "national treatment" works both ways. He said: "Goods from Manitoba will be treated exactly the same as goods from Minnesota". However, that is only half of the equation because goods from Minnesota will also be treated like goods from Manitoba, in Manitoba. That has tremendous implications for both federal and provincial procurement policies and subsidies, marketing boards, and tax incentives to business.
Yesterday, in her interview, the Minister for International Trade said that the negotiators have not discussed the subject. Who do we believe, the Prime Minister who talked about national treatment about which there is nothing in the motion before the House, or the Minister with her statement to journalists yesterday on television?
We had hoped that today we would finally get a clear statement from the Prime Minister about what is at stake in these negotiations. Rather than hear that statement, we have more uncertainty and more confusion.
How will Canadians adjust? Will there be adjustment assistance for industries, for our workers, and for our regions? Is the phase-in period 12 years, 10 years, five years, or two years? Where are the training programs for our workers and our young people and those men and women in their 40s and 50s who, through no fault of their own, are displaced by technological change or potentially by a trade arrangement?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I regret to interrupt the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner). Considering the time and the fact that we have not heard from the Leader of the New Democratic Party, I wonder whether the House might not be disposed to sit through the normal lunch hour.
Why did you not do that when he was finished?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I would have waited until he was finished but we only had a minute left. I regret having to interrupt the Hon. Leader.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) has suggested that the Chair not see the clock. That is what the House has done continually in the past. I gather there is agreement to that. The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner).

Mr. Speaker, I do not take umbrage with the Deputy Prime Minister's proper intervention.
What is happening to our educational system and research and development? The Government has consistently cut training programs and has cut its commitment to postsecondary education. That is wrong, regardless of a free trade agreement. Any trading arrangement will not repair the lack of our ability to compete because of our lack of development in research, education, and apprenticeship. If the Government

March 16, 1987
Bilateral Trade
assumes that great opportunities will flow from a trade agreement, how will we capitalize on those opportunities if our workforce lacks the expertise and skills and the required training?
A trade agreement is no substitute for a lack of national economic policy. It is no substitute for a national economic policy on productivity, on working to make us more competitive, on getting us to work smarter and think smarter and to compete around the world. This Government has abandoned that kind of policy, putting all its eggs in one basket by relying on increased U.S. trade as the sole salvation of our economy.
The Liberal Party's trade policy is to fight hard to ensure that any agreement with the United States does not limit those opportunities, or limit our political independence as a nation. Bringing us closer together economically has its risks in terms of our sovereignty, the independence of our foreign policy, our culture, social programs and our regional economic equality. These are important to us. We do not want them negotiated away. I have spoken on two or three other occasions on this trade matter when we had to set the agenda ourselves with our own motions. We enjoy the type of uniqueness and distinction of living on the northern half of this continent with a separate political system, separate traditions, a multicultural mosaic, two official languages and a limitless inheritance in terms of the environment.
