We like doing things our way. Yet we are an outward looking nation. We do not believe in fortress Canada. We look outward. I do not believe we would feel comfortable in fortress North America. I think we have to be very, very careful as to how we analyse this situation. We respect our American neighbours. We value them as trading partners. However, we will not bargain away our rights as Canadians to control our own destiny.
It is for all these reasons that I present the following amendment to the Government's motion. I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy):
That the Motion be amended by deleting all of the words after the word "arrangement" and by substituting the following:
"or arrangements with the United States, as part of Canada's multilateral trade policy, while protecting Canadian sovereignly through the application of the following conditions.
Namely that:
There not be an all-inclusive free trade arrangement with the United States since such an arrangement would undermine Canada's political, economic and cultural independence; and would jeopardize Canada's regional development policies, agricultural policies, cultural industries, financial service industries, and the Auto Pact;
And that:
Any such negotiations are designed to gain greater access to U.S. markets by limiting the operation of contingency protection and non-tariff barriers such as current U.S. and State government procurement regulations and restoring previous access for softwood lumber in U.S. markets;
While at the same time:
Ensuring Canadian independence for domestic programs, policies and legislative authority in areas such as: social policy, agricultural marketing.
supply management and support programs; subsidies and assistance for regional and industrial development programs including high technology development; the Auto Pact; the environment; bilingualism (including labelling); culture (including cultural industries); financial and service industries;
And that:
The Government of Canada tables transitional adjustment assistance proposals to protect those workers, sectors, firms and businesses which may be adversely affected by such a trading arrangement or arrangements;
And that:
The Government of Canada secure an immediate standstill of U.S. trade harassment including such matters as agriculture, energy, fish, potash, and steel."

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) has completed his address. The House has agreed to not see the clock and we will be looking to the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) to speak on behalf of the New Democratic Party. In the meantime, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition has proposed a motion, seconded by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). I think I should indicate to the House now that the obligation of the Chair is to examine the motion to see that it is in order and to report back as soon as it is appropriate. In the meantime, it is my suggestion that the debate continue and I would recognize the Hon. Member for Oshawa.

Mr. Speaker, the central Canadian reality in terms of political and economic relationships is, of course, the relationship we have with the United States of America. Therefore, any measure which comes before the Parliament of Canada which directly impinges upon that relationship in a significant way has to be one which is treated with utmost seriousness by members of all Parties on both sides of the House.
Two years ago the Government of Canada launched a major initiative in terms of its proposed change in economic relationships between Canada and the United States. During the intervening period, serious questions have been raised about the implications of that course of direction on Canadian life. Quite specifically, simply to cite the motion we have before us today, questions have been raised about Canadian sovereignty, about the impact on Canadian agriculture, on our cultural industries, on the automotive sector, and one could extend the list. The impact on almost every aspect of Canadian existence is involved in such a trade relationship, and serious questions have been raised in the last two years about the expansion of this trade relationship.
This debate, in terms of historical comparisons, appropriately ought to raise in Canadian minds the great historical debates we witnessed in this country going back to the founding of our nation, debates involving Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Wilfrid Laurier and, in different circumstances in the post-war period, debates which have involved Lester Pearson and John Diefenbaker. I say this because, in my judgment, those debates addressed in a serious way historical concerns. I had hoped on behalf of the people of Canada that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) got to his feet today,
March 16, 1987

he would have understood what was required of a Prime Minister at this particular juncture in our history and in the discussions of these trade talks, and tell us what was going on in terms of the specifics of the impacts on our culture, on sovereignty, on agriculture, and on the automotive industry. We thought we might get some details. We did not get any.
The implications for me are simply twofold. Either the Prime Minister knew and decided not to share the information with the people of Canada or perhaps, and I am not sure it is more regrettable but equally regrettable, the Government does not know what is really involved in terms of the intricacies of the impact in all these areas. In either case, the Prime Minister and the Government, in these major discussions up to this point, are failing completely the aspirations of the people of Canada.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, and all Hon. Members of the House, to consider the second part of this resolution which strikes me as significant. First, there is the content, the specific wording, and the reference to particular areas of concern Canadians would have about entering into a comprehensive free trade arrangement. That is fundamentally the substance of an arrangement we would have to consider. The other aspect of the resolution is that the Parliament of Canada at this particular point in 1987 is being asked to authorize the Government to pursue the course of direction it launched in this important and economic political matter some two years ago.
What we have is a Prime Minister who has abolished FIRA, who has sold out Prentice Hall, who has caved in on softwood, who has given away fishing rights in Atlantic Canada, who has yielded to the United States on acid rain, who has sacrificed our generic drug industry and who is now coming to the Parliament of Canada and asking for a blank cheque to continue this approach to Canadian politics. I can tell him that we will not give him that blank cheque.
Hear, hear!

I say quite frankly, the first five to 10 minutes of the Prime Minister's speech were what one might expect of a Prime Minister. It was sober in tone. It began to intimate that there would be some answers provided to the serious questions that ought to be addressed by Parliament. Then, for another 30 or 40 minutes, we heard what can only be described as a kind of high-school-cum-Rotary-Club rhetoric that is totally inappropriate to the seriousness of this occasion-totally inappropriate.
Before I deal with the substance of the resolution that is before us and address on behalf of my Party some of the concerns that we have about some of those specifics, I want to take up the Prime Minister's challenge which he made to us part way through his speech. He said that he would like to see what the opposition Parties would put in its place. I think the whole country has noted that the Prime Minister has said that
Bilateral Trade
as justification for this initiative that he launched two years ago we have but one of two options. They are to face massive unemployment on the one hand, or to select this Conservative option on the other. It is an old mug's game. It is a rhetorical device by which one has to choose one or other of the options. Anyone who has thought seriously about anything knows that there are almost always more than two choices in any situation.
I wish to say to the Prime Minister, categorically, before I say something on trade, that I agree with him and any thoughtful person in this country who says that trade is important to Canada. Indeed, one of the crucial ways of expanding employment opportunities in Canada is to extend our trade opportunities, and I also say in this context, trade not simply with the United States, which is important, but also with the Pacific Rim and many other parts of the world. I wish to stress this. On behalf of the unemployed people of the country I find it intellectually unacceptable and morally offensive to suggest that the only way we can deal with unemployment is by way of a major trade initiative.
The Prime Minister cited the Government of Manitoba in his speech. I wish to tell him that I am proud that Manitoba has the lowest unemployment rate in Canada today. I want to tell him also that that was not done by expanding trade initiatives. It was done as a result of a Government which believes in the mixed economy and in the social democratic approach. It believes that one has to have job creation, and it set out to create jobs for the people of Manitoba.
Hear, hear!

In this context, because it is so germane to the central justification for what the Prime Minister says about trade, I also want to point to another Government in Canada which, not relying on the primacy of a trade thrust, also dealt with unemployment in the last couple of years. I refer to the Government of Yukon. It is a New Democratic Government as well.
I hear snickers from members opposite. It happened to be the case when the NDP Government came to power that there was an unemployment rate in Yukon of about 20 per cent. But because the Government believed in initiatives other than those directly based on trade, unemployment was cut by 50 per cent in one year.
Hear, hear!
Oh, oh!

I say to the snickering Conservatives opposite that no matter what country in the world we consider or what region of Canada we consider, if there is a Government in place which is concerned about unemployment, then there are many options other than the trade option with respect to creating jobs to consider.

March 16, 1987
Bilateral Trade
I now wish to talk about the trade option itself. I am not saying that it is the exclusive way to promote jobs but that it is indeed an important way.

Mr. Speaker, we of the New Democratic Party agree that the United States is and always will be our most important trading partner. Ninety per cent of our exports now enter the United States duty free. That is the situation today, and I think we should try and obtain sectorial agreements with the United States that would benefit both parties. We have one example the Prime Minister has often referred to in the past, namely the Auto Pact, and if we can have similar agreements in other sectors, we would like to take this particular one as a model.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, I say we should try and establish a process for settling bilateral disputes so as to restrict the arbitrary levying of compensatory measures by both parties.
Mr. Speaker, I am saying restrict, not eliminate altogether.

In this context I wish to say that if I understood the Leader of the Opposition correctly, it seems to me that in any trade arrangement with the Americans, if we want to protect our sovereignty and respect their sovereignty, it will be impossible, and ought to be impossible, for us to eliminate entirely the right of either nation at some point to take countervailing action against the other.
I think I used the word "restriction".

The Leader of the Opposition is now saying that he believes in restricting that right. If so, then we are in agreement. But we in this Party believe that important steps ought to be taken to establish a bilateral mechanism, something about which all Parties in the House have talked, which could reduce the immediacy of such actions by the other country and eliminate or reduce the range in which countervailing steps can be taken. That would be very useful indeed. We in this Party believe in the sovereignty of Canada and the ultimate obligation we have to make the economic decisions which affect our people, and we know that that is reciprocal. So at some time if we say that we have the right to take economic actions to protect the interests of our people, then we must concede right away that we could not expect the United States to eliminate entirely the right to take action to protect its own citizens. That is a given right.
Having said that, I also want to add that we believe that, in addition to expanding trade with the United States, which I have already said is our most important trading partner, we have to make great efforts to expand trade with other countries. In this context one of the very serious concerns on the part of many provinces which have thought seriously about a special bilateral deal with the United States is that their export arrangements with other countries could be adversely affected. In this context I am thinking particularly of our western
provinces which have important export markets in addition to the United States. I know that there is a deep and genuine concern on their part about the possible effects of a bilateral arrangement made exclusively with the United States which could lead to the reduction or elimination of contracts they now have with other countries outside North America. That is a matter which has to be considered with a great deal of seriousness by the Government of Canada.
Third, in terms of job creation and economic growth, we must begin as a nation to make a serious effort to get away from the massive dependence that we now have on the export of resources and semi-processed goods, whether it be to the United States or to other countries. It has to be and ought to be a major matter of industrial policy in Canada to shift our nation away, to use an old cliche, from being hewers of wood and drawers of water to a policy that begins to use more of our resources as a foundation for manufacturing the goods here in Canada and exporting those goods abroad.
Hear, hear!

This specifically ought to entail duplicating in Canada what has been done by other industrial nations in the process of their development, whether one thinks of the United States, Germany, Great Britain or in more recent times Japan, namely, to look systematically at certain sectors for import replacement. Where we have a disproportionate amount of manufactured imports coming in, in certain sectors, we should, if we have an appropriate research and development and an investment strategy, be able to replace those imports with domestically produced manufactured goods. We could then use that enhanced domestic market as a foundation for exporting manufactured goods abroad. That is the longer range strategy. It is one we ought to have had in place decades ago and it is one we need now.
The next aspect of a trade strategy that we see as being appropriate, in addition to expanding our trade relations with the U.S., is one which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) indeed talked about just a few minutes ago, namely, to put more emphasis on the GATT. Not only is it desirable in this world of ours, with many Third World nations in utter destitution, to do everything we can to expand trade on a multi-lateral equitable basis, but I say, particularly in the context of our relationships with the U.S., we can get greater access, to put it more precisely-we have good access now-to the U.S. market by taking effective action through the GATT where we are working with other smaller nations like ourselves in terms of economic power in comparative terms with the United States.
I would say in that context to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney)-I do not always give him a reading list to look at-that perhaps he could look at some of the better works of Machiavelli, not the usual vulgar interpretation of Machiavelli that are referred to. He wrote interestingly and appropriately, given our relationship with the United States, about the
March 16, 1987

dangers of a weaker prince entering into a forum and a binding alliance with the stronger prince. When we have limited economic clout, no matter how effective and determined we are in using that, I say to the Prime Minister that we have to be very wary indeed of linking that holus-bolus to the United States, to put it rather directly. We need more emphasis on a multilateral approach in terms of broadening not only our trade with other nations but ultimately to gain greater and more equitable access to the U.S. market.

Fifth, Mr. Speaker, we need some vigorous research in this country to develop more policies for economic self-sufficiency, designed for the purpose of using our market to implement effective job creation policies. That is to say, we could have federal plans for the creation of new jobs established along the same lines as what the Government of Yukon and the Government of Manitoba have already set up in this country.

These are some important initiatives that would expand our trade opportunities. They would give us not only greater commerce but for us, what is the fundamental objective, a greater number of jobs.
The Prime Minister asked for some suggestions. I would be happy to pass on to him a resolution passed during our convention in the last few days from which points have been drawn about expanding trade. I ask him to have a hard look at it and I ask him to pass it to his officials. I am sure they are looking at other resolutions with a great deal of interest, but I ask them to look at this one with care, and perhaps if they adopted some of the measures recommended the Prime Minister would see that there is an option to putting all our eggs in the American basket for economic development.
Having briefly indicated some of the other approaches that ought to be pursued, I want now to address the wording of the resolution in some of its key elements, to express our concern about the Government's direction in this major economic initiative. I have already indicated what I think is our central concern, namely, the Prime Minister's own attitude toward the United States, as has been demonstrated in a whole range of bilateral matters in the past two years. I say frankly that the New Democratic Party simply does not have confidence in the Prime Minister as the principal negotiator with the United States of America.
I want also to say something about the evidence that we have accumulated so far in Canada, that has at least been publicly available, that ought to make Canadians rationally, reasonably concerned about moving into a free trade arrangement with the United States. The Prime Minister did not today present us with new information that might have influenced the decision in a more positive direction, as he would define it. He did not do that, so we have to rely on what has already come out. What has come out frankly is not encouraging. We have had a federal study that was censored very substantially. But even when one sets aside the censured
Bilateral Trade
nature of that document, we found some rather alarming figures. For example, 900,000 workers in Canada would be directly affected by a new arrangement of the magnitude about which the Government of Canada is talking. The Ontario study showed that in Ontario alone some 281,000 jobs were in what was described, perhaps euphemistically, as the sensitive sectors. That does not even include the 125,000 men and women who work in the automotive sector.
In the Province of Quebec, we know from another study, some 30,000 textile workers directly would be impacted upon, not to mention in that province other workers that we know would be seriously concerned. I am thinking of the clothing industry, the shoe industry and the shipbuilding industry.
To my knowledge, the significant studies on which we have information to base a judgment that I have now alluded to, are the federal Government study, the Government of Ontario study, and the Government of Quebec study. The empirical evidence, I repeat, that we do have ought to make us reticent and ought to give us pause about entering into this kind of an arrangement. Why should we, when we have one million already unemployed, risk putting out on the streets thousands more Canadian workers?
I see another member shaking his head. The implication is that he disagrees with the facts I have given. But the facts I have given have come from three governments, none of them NDP governments. They are their studies, not mine. I also say to the member that if the Prime Minister has counter evidence, instead of giving us broad macro figures about the jobs we might get from a new free trade arrangement, why does he not produce the studies? Why does he not come here and say, "Here is the evidence. In this sector we will have this many new jobs and in that sector we will have that many"? He has not produced the evidence. I say to the Prime Minister that as long as the evidence we have available is negative, as it seems in its implications, we must hesitate to get into this kind of arrangement with the United States.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I think there would be a disposition on our side to allow the Hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party to continue his remarks beyond the normal 20-minute period.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is that agreeable?

I appreciate the gesture, Mr. Speaker.
Our second concern relates to the historical nature of the Canadian economy and a continuing ongoing problem. The reality is that, compared with other industrial or quasiindustrial nations, we have a disproportionate amount of foreign ownership in our economy. Let us look at a variety of sectors. I have some figures. The current data on mining

March 16, 1987
Bilateral Trade
indicates 35 per cent; oil and gas, 40 per cent; and manufacturing, 45 per cent. The implications, in terms of the consequences of entering into a continentalized economic arrangement with the United States, are that these firms, most of which are owned in the United States, could very well have a major economic reason to move their branch plants back to the United States, if not this year, at least in two years. It does not assume that they are sinister. It does not assume that they are plotting against Canadian interests. All it assumes is for them to be what they are-profit-making business organizations. If they can make more money by moving a branch plant from Michigan to Georgia, it is not foolish to think that they may believe it is more economically sensible to move the branch plant out of Oakville or Hamilton or someplace in British Columbia or Manitoba.
If we tear down the border economically and all its implications, with no requirement for a certain level of investment in Canada, why would these firms not move to the greater market in size, which is the United States, not Canada? Again we have serious reasons to doubt the wisdom of the policy of the Government in this regard.
Another concern which we have-and I mentioned it earlier-is that of our trading partners. I happened to speak with the leader of one of the provincial Governments concerned about export markets to other countries than the United States if we have a bilateral agreement only with the United States. The concern is that the export, in this particular instance of raw materials, could be jeopardized if the third trading country thinks that we will have a preferential relationship of some kind with the United States from which it is excluded.
Another concern would be the kind of bilateral mechanism which would be set up to inhibit countervail action on either side of the border. As the Prime Minister knows very well, in the free trade agreement between Israel and the United States, the United States has retained ultimate sovereign control; its right to take countervail action. As I said a few minutes ago, I understand that because my Party and I believe Canada must ultimately retain that control too. If we believe that, the exact nature of the mechanism being discussed between the two parties now is something about which we would like to know a lot. It is something that one would have hoped the Prime Minister would have informed the people of Canada through Parliament today, so that we could have some real understanding of where in terms of this institution we may be heading.
Now I want to talk about the areas of concern which are addressed or named in the resolution. I have some concerns about which I wanted to hear the Prime Minister speak, but did not. Social programs were referred to. In general terms there will be protection of our social programs. We want to know about some of them specifically, not the general phrase. In most aspects in life it is the specifics which count, not the general observations.
In this regard we know that in recent trade disputes the Americans have objected to unemployment insurance benefits
for our fishermen. They have regarded those-and they have argued it-as a form of subsidy. Will we have assurances that whatever form of unemployment insurance we have in Canada will not be affected by a trade agreement between Canada, it and the United States? That is very important to us, and again we learned nothing about it today.
Agricultural marketing is profoundly important to at least half our provinces as a crucial sector of their economy. I want to be very specific about a concern which has been raised with me in this regard. It is one thing to talk about protecting marketing boards, but what may well be involved-and I will be very frank-and what I suspect is involved is that the Government will say marketing boards will be kept but the supply-management side of marketing will go, that there will be no control of imports coming from the United States to these sectors.
Oh, oh!

I hear some questioning from the back that that would not be the case. All I can say is that we in this Party are concerned about protecting the interests of farmers. If they are to maintain marketing boards, including the supply-management side, the Prime Minister should have risen to his feet today and told us about it. It is important to farmers producing eggs, poultry, and milk to know where the Government stands on that.
It is also important to refer to another item. I see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise). I hope he will join in the debate. The Minister knows that seasonal tariffs are applied in Canada to protect fruits and vegetables at certain times. Will the new agreement which is to be talked about with the United States enable our farmers during particular seasons to have the important protection needed from those tariffs? We want to ensure that they are protected. We want to hear from the Government of Canada on it.
Also we are concerned about the auto industry. We are concerned that once again we may have the form of the agreement protected but the substance gutted. The Canada-U.S. automotive pact has two key elements. One is investment requirement and the second is the threat of tariffs or duties if major automotive producers do not live up to their automotive investment requirements. As the Ministers responsible know, that has worked out reasonably well.
However, I will tell the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), who is following this debate, that not many days ago I talked with a senior officer of one of the largest automotive companies in Canada. I asked him what would be his response if the Government of Canada kept the Canada-U.S. automotive agreement, said that there should be a certain level of investment on an annual basis in Canada, and at the same time removed all tariffs and duties. I said, "Would that not be an incentive for you to begin transferring all your industry back to the United States and, instead of producing here, starting to export across the tariff-free border from the United States?" I say frankly that there was a pause on the
March 16, 1987

end of the line. The person with whom I talked was quite honest, and he said, "Yes, you are right; there would be an economic incentive to move the industry out of Canada and back to the United States".
That is no laughing or joking matter. If the Government is to indulge in a bogus game of saying that it will keep the formal requirements of the pact which talk about investment levels but remove the negative incentive, if I can put it that way, of tariffs and duties if they do not live up to their requirements, we in this country could see before the end of the century the complete obliteration-and I put it as strongly as that-of the North American automotive industry.
Again I say to the Government, if it has guarantees on the pact, and if it is to maintain the basic structure including the mechanism of the threat to use tariffs and duties if investment is not lived up, then the Prime Minister ought to have told us about that today.
Another subject mentioned in the resolution which I had hoped the Prime Minister would have addressed is our cultural identity. All of us in the House can agree on the cliche that the cultural identity of Canada must be preserved. It is a cliche but it is also reality. I would like to believe all members wish to preserve it. There are all kinds of uniquely important and distinctive aspects to French-Canadian cultural heritage and to English-Canadian cultural heritage which are monthly gaining greater and greater international recognition.
We also know that important protective mechanisms have been put in place in Canada through the years to ensure the survival and growth of Canada's creative people. I say that it is not enough to talk about the protection of cultural identity and uniqueness in this context without talking about the protection of cultural industries. There is nothing in the resolution that refers to cultural industries. Once again, if the Prime Minister had been forthcoming and had wanted to allay some concerns, rather than raising new ones, he would have told us what the Government plans to do with cultural industries.
Another question which looms as a very important concern in terms of the resolution and what flows out of it is what will happen during the phase-in period of such a trade agreement. If we have no FIRA, no effective instrument to protect highly creative, quite profitable, in the Canadian context, and in many cases technically sophisticated industries during this phase-in period, what will stop these companies from being gobbled up by larger companies with more capital resources from the United States? If there is to be a 10-year phase-in period that is supposed to make allowances for adjustments in agriculture and the labour market, setting aside all reservations I have raised about that, what will happen to the ownership of our industries? At the end of the 10-year period, rather than having 25 per cent, 30 per cent or 40 per cent of industries in certain categories American-owned, that figure could double.
Bilateral Trade
After the gobbling up process has begun, the pattern in this kind of international economic development is that an American company first buys a competitor, a good, small Canadian firm, and then operates it as a branch plant for a while. Then the company moves operations back to the United States. We are very concerned about this 10-year, or whatever the magic figure might be, phase-in period and its impact on good, innovative, imaginative Canadian firms that happen to be smaller in size and could be gobbled up by American competitors. The New Democratic Party would not put in motion any kind of resolution that could lead to that. We think, however, that the Government of Canada could do precisely that.
I would like to conclude my observations with a remark made by an earlier Prime Minister, one of the greatest and perhaps the greatest Prime Minister Canada has ever had. For someone living in 19th century Canada, Sir John A. Macdonald had imagination and vision about what needed to be done to build a country. I did not expect to see a social democrat as a Prime Minister in the 19th century, as bizarre as that might sound. One looks for a range of criteria for praising people, and I do not say glibly at all that Sir John A. Macdonald was a great Canadian. His remarks are pertinent to today's debate because in the latter part of the 19th century, he had a choice. There were many voices and arguments saying that we should develop one country in North America and that there should not be a border. They said that rather than expanding to the West, Upper and Lower Canada and what are now the Maritime Provinces ought to join with the United States and there should be one continental country.
Sir John A. Macdonald had a different view, and in retrospect, I say thank God for that. In an important debate in the House of Commons held on March 7, 1878, he said that "there are national considerations that rise far higher than the mere accumulation of wealth, than the mere question of trade advantage. There is," he said, "national status, national dominion and, he concluded, no great nation has ever risen whose policy was free trade." He was right.
Sir John A. Macdonald then went on to talk about Great Britain. Great Britain did not achieve greatness on the basis of free trade. Neither did the United States, nor Japan. The great industrial nations in history have talked about free trade only after they have dominated the economic world. That is the reality.
Sir John A. Macdonald had an appropriate vision. Put in modern terms, he said that Canada had to be something other than a cash register and that there is more to human existence than that. I happen to believe that the modern equivalent of the range of policies needed for our nation, both in economic and social terms, happen to be social democratic in nature. I happen to believe that the kind of political and economic framework provided by social democracy, with a mixed economy using proudly and effectively the instruments of both the private and the public sectors, is the right one. We must proceed with confidence as a starting point and we must have a

March 16, 1987
national development strategy that makes it important for men and women to get jobs while expanding trade. In the final analysis, such a policy says that we have to protect our culture, we have to protect our industries and we have to protect our sovereignty. That is what the Party I happen to lead is all about. It is that kind of political and economic thrust we think is necessary. For that reason, we are completely opposed to the motion before us.

Mr. Speaker, the rules provide for a 10-minute question and comment period but I would suggest that in view of the healthy debate we have had on this motion to this point, and our side has no questions or comments, unless members of the New Democratic Party or the Liberal Party wish to engage in same, I would think the House could recess until two o'clock.
Agreed.

subsubtopic: POSSIBLE IMPACT OF CANADA-UNITED STATES PROPOSED TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government claims that a free trade deal will be struck with the U.S. but Canadians still do not know whether such an agreement could affect the environment. In 1986 the Canadian Environmental Advisory Council and the Desfosses report warned the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) about the trade agreement having an impact on the environment.
A free trade agreement could generate pressure by business, particularly multinationals, on government to reduce the cost of environmental regulation. An agreement could seriously hinder federal and provincial measures on controlling point sources of pollution, hazardous waste management, reforestation, fisheries management, waste water treatment and air quality, because the U.S. could interpret such measures as a form of subsidy. The Minister has not yet realized the gravity of the situation. It is of the greatest urgency and I urge him, as
I did on May 6, 1986, to ensure that a trade agreement with the U.S. will not have a negative impact on Canada's environment.

subtopic: IMPORTANCE OF ACCESS TO NORTH AMERICAN MARKETS
IMPORTANCE OF ACCESS TO NORTH AMERICAN MARKETS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my constituents in Nepean-Carleton have long recognized the importance of research and development and its contribution to our economic well-being. That interest has allowed Nepean-Carleton to become the high technology centre for Canada. My constituents therefore welcomed the signing last week of the historic landmark agreement between the provinces and the federal Government on a science policy for Canada.
Canada's high technology companies are developing world mandates and must compete internationally. Access to North American markets is fundamental and vital. To move forward with a trade agreement, while enhancing our agricultural industry by protecting our agricultural marketing system, will benefit all Canadians, especially young Canadians, because trade is the pathway to our future prosperity.

subtopic: ADOPTION OF RESOLUTION RECOGNIZING UNIQUE CHARACTER OF QUEBEC
ADOPTION OF RESOLUTION RECOGNIZING UNIQUE CHARACTER OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
Over the weekend, Mr. Speaker, the New Democratic Party of Canada adopted a resolution acknowledging the unique character of Quebec, where French is the language and culture of the majority. From Victoria in British Columbia to St. John's in Newfoud-land, including the Prairies, Ontario and the Maritimes, the New Democrats said yes to Quebec. On the federal scene ours is the political Party which shows the most open-minded approach to Quebec.
It is deplorable and regrettable that the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) should adopt such a partisan attitude. If acknowledging the uniqueness of Quebec is a trick, as claimed by the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides, how are we going to qualify last November's decision of the Liberal Party of Canada not to acknowledge this unique character of Quebec, as indeed it has always refused to acknowledge in the past?
March 16, 1987

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-IMPORTANCE OF CONCLUDING AGREEMENT
CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-IMPORTANCE OF CONCLUDING AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in today's competitive global market where protectionism is becoming the norm, it is imperative that Canada conclude a free trade agreement with the U.S. if we are to remain a major industrial power. Canada needs a secure market for our products if it is to remain prosperous. Trade is the only vehicle by which Canadians can continue to enjoy economic prosperity. Canadian employment and survival depend on our ability to sell our products.
Not too long ago, in a parallel situation, European countries were addressing the same problems we are today. They formed the EEC which guaranteed secure markets for their products. This economic union allowed those nations to become major economic entities which have produced a standard of living equivalent to that of Canada. Each one of those nations addressed the problem of sovereignty, as well as cultural and economic domination. Yet after 30 years that economic union has become a major economic force with four members being part of the G-7 group of countries. A free trade pact with the U.S. is the only method to ensure that present and future generations can continue to enjoy economic prosperity.

Mr. Speaker, more than 70 Quebec independent consumer organizations cover the province, including 25 which make up three distinct federations. A number of task forces are working to find solutions and take action to help Quebec consumers.
After analysing the new program and funding allotment criteria, I concluded that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) has a tendency to ignore the decentralized operations of Quebec consumer organizations and their particular way of working.
In 1986-87, two national organizations which are practically inactive in Quebec account for 72 per cent of the funding allotted by the Minister. When setting aside 15.5 per cent of the budget for Quebec associations, the Minister advised them the funding was transitory and final.
In case the situation grows even worse next year, and to improve the situation this year, I urge the Minister to look into this problem at the earliest opportunity.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-SUPPORT FOR POSSIBLE AGREEMENT
CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-SUPPORT FOR POSSIBLE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a freer trade agreement between Canada and the U.S. will mean economic growth for Canada and new jobs for Canadians. The Economic Council of Canada estimates that a freer trade agreement will mean about 370,000 new jobs by 1995. Without that agreement, Canada stands to lose over 500,000 jobs by that same date due to American protectionism.
There is also no doubt that a freer trade agreement will benefit western Canada. A study by the Canada West Foundation indicates that one in every five dollars in the western Canadian economy depends directly on sales to the U.S. A study done by the prairie pools indicates a freer trade agreement with the U.S. would mean an extra $60 million a year for prairie farmers. With a built-in guarantee of protection for marketing boards and institutions like the Wheat Board, western Canadian farmers have much to gain and very little to lose from a freer trade agreement.
For over 100 years western Canada has been asking for a freer trade agreement with the U.S. but its interests have always been thwarted by central Canadian protectionism. Once again we are at the crossroads and I believe western Canada wants us to move ahead so that we, too, can benefit from the growth occurring in Canada today.

subtopic: HONDURAS-EFFECT OF AMERICAN MILITARY PRESENCE ON ECONOMY
HONDURAS-EFFECT OF AMERICAN MILITARY PRESENCE ON ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in spite of massive aid from Canada and the U.S., Honduras continues to be one of the poorest countries in South and Central America. The American military presence in that country has created a vast network of roads, air fields and storage facilities which distort the economy and only reflect Ronald Reagan's paranoia about the struggling nation of Nicaragua. These military installations, and the American-supported Contra bases, have done nothing to alleviate the poverty, hunger, unemployment, and underdevelopment of the countryside. We now learn that over the past five years one-third of the $1 billion in U.S. aid has been diverted from economic development into the pockets of Honduran military officials.
No amount of aid can help a nation on the road to development if the Government does not have the right priorities. Because Canada is a significant donor to Honduras we have a major responsibility to Canadian taxpayers as well as to the people of Honduras to pressure the U.S. to cease using

March 16, 1987
Elonduras as a military platform, with all its attendant corruption, and allow Honduras and the other countries of Central America to follow their own path of development in peace.

subtopic: NEED FOR SERIOUS CONSIDERATION OF LIBERALIZATION OF EXCHANGES WITH UNITED STATES
NEED FOR SERIOUS CONSIDERATION OF LIBERALIZATION OF EXCHANGES WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are now striding towards the 21st century. Our future is that of a peace-loving and prosperous nation that aims for excellence. A nation that thanks to the vigour of its economy will be able to provide for the well-being of its people, the full development of its cultural identity and maintain its sovereignty.
Free trade with the United States is something we should seriously consider. The people of Beauce have understood. Forty-six per cent of our products are distributed elsewhere in this country and 39 per cent of our manufactured goods are exported outside Canada, especially to the United States. The people of Beauce will have much to gain from free trade. Our entrepreneurs have understood the need for diversifying their products and taking advantage of foreign markets, and this attitude has made our region one of the most dynamic in the country.
Not long ago I was reading an article in the Reader's Digest about the "beauceron miracle", and we can be proud of the image of quality and performance we project.
The economist and Harvard professor John Kenneth Galbraith said it so well: "A country cannot isolate itself from the rest of the world and solve all of its problems alone, away from the international context, because all countries have become interdependent".

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) should immediately put a halt to deportation procedures against Salvadorian journalist Victor Regalado. Knowing with what one is charged and being able to defend oneself against those charges is one of the basic principles of our legal system. Mr. Regalado was not given that opportunity.
Changes in the Immigration Act that were made in 1984 now allow for review of a security statement by a monitoring committee of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service.
Mr. Speaker, the Act was amended to allow for situations like that of Mr. Regalado but does not apply to him because his case dates back to before the Act came into effect. Mr. Regalado is the victim of a procedural default which should now be corrected. I want to ask the Minister of Immigration to stop deportation procedures against Mr. Regalado and put his case before the monitoring committee, where he can take advantage of all the recourse and protection afforded under Canadian law.

subtopic: EFFECT OF TARIFFS ON PETROCHEMICAL INDUSTRY
EFFECT OF TARIFFS ON PETROCHEMICAL INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, nearly 40 per cent of the country's petrochemical industry is located in the constituency of Sarnia-Lambton. The global marketplace is of the utmost importance to the jobs and livelihoods of the residents of Sarnia-Lambton. The petrochemical industries in my constituency do not need a long phase-in period for free trade with the United States. They are ready for it now.
Polysar, the single largest employer in my constituency, exports 21 per cent of its product to the United States. It is of concern that at present the tariff on styrene trade across the U.S. border is about 7.4 per cent. Clearly without the tariff hurdle the market for Canadian petrochemical plants in the United States would be greatly expanded. The money saved by our companies in tariffs could be utilized to cover higher transportation costs to expand further in the American market.
It is a fact that Canadian companies can compete globally, but tariffs limit their sales in the United States. The direction the Government is heading is the right one. We want jobs for Canadians and greater investment in Canada by foreign companies.

Mr. Speaker, is CTV going to close its Winnipeg and Quebec City offices? Are the firings in news staffs it has begun going to become massacre? We do not know for sure yet, but we do know, as the Caplan-Sauvageau Report documents, that CTV manages to look poor by a fancy bookkeeping arrangement that enables its affiliates to make a bundle. Any claim that CTV might now make that it is losing money and has to cut Canadian program staff should not be believed.
March 16, 1987

CTV has a lot of nerve. News coverage has been the only area where Canadian programming has been remotely adequate. The CRTC is now considering the CTV licence renewal and Canadians are hoping that increased Canadian content will be required. In cutting news staff the CTV is thumbing its nose at the CRTC and the Canadian public for whom it works.
The firings must stop. If ever there were a time for the CRTC to get tough, it is now. If CTV cannot better its Canadian content, it does not deserve a place on the Canadian public's airwaves.

Mr. Speaker, over the past few weeks we have heard a good deal about the defensive reasons for a new trading arrangement with the United States. There is no question that these are important. What interests me even more, however, is the offence. I hear from my colleagues on the left and those further left that Canada cannot compete. Their comments are covered with rhetoric and chocolate coating, but the bottom line is that they believe Canadians cannot compete, that we would get the worst of a trading arrangement with the United States, that the Americans would take over Canada.
What a tragedy that two of the three political Parties in Canada have no faith in our technology, no faith in our working people, no faith in our management, and, indeed, appear to have no faith in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, students throughout Canada are fighting the Government's cut-backs in funding of post-secondary education. In my province, students at the University of Prince Edward Island are burdened with tuition fees which are among the highest in the country. The Government's plans to limit funding increases for postsecondary education under the Established Programs Financing structure will worsen an already abhorrent situation.
This year University of Prince Edward Island students will pay about $1,480 tuition plus other mandatory fees, book costs, and living expenses. Students are struggling with inadequate facilities, overcrowded classrooms and labs, and insufficient course offerings in some programs. Clearly these difficulties affect the quality of education which a student
receives. I ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Government to rethink these cut-backs and look upon educating our young people as an astute investment in Canada's future.

maintopic: CONFIDENCE IN CANADIANS' ABILITY TO COMPETE INTERNATIONALLY
CONFIDENCE IN CANADIANS' ABILITY TO COMPETE INTERNATIONALLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is time we asked ourselves some tough questions. Are we afraid of our ability to compete fairly with the rest of the world? Should Canadian consumers continue to pay $6 billion every year for import restrictions? Is there some inherent reason why Canadians must fail when presented with the opportunity to triumph? The answer to every one of these questions must be a firm, confident, and aggressive "No".
I make no apology for my confidence in our ability to compete fairly. I make no apology for my belief that the best of Canadian talent, the best of our workers, our managers, our entrepreneurs, will prosper. I make no apology for my desire for a Canadian economy which finds its survival in strength, not in fear. I make no apology, Mr. Speaker, for my confidence that we can and will find a new and dynamic equilibrium in free trade to replace the economic inertia of an economy based on import restrictions and small markets.
Canada has the opportunity now to grab the future and shape it to our needs, to take the tides of change and channel them to our advantage. We can retreat if we are afraid. We can, like the NDP, hide behind psychological barricades, but we cannot hide from the world forever.

Mr. Speaker, according to the Auditor of the Province of Ontario the provincial court-house in L'Orignal in my riding is so deficient that witnesses must wait for trials in the same rooms as the accused, and is so unsafe that prisoners, juries and judges are at risk from fire. That is, of course, from 40-odd years of Tory neglect at the provincial level.
Today I want to make a formal demand for a grant under the new federal IOU program, since my riding qualifies under the same criteria used in the riding of Central Nova for the building of a court-house there. I take this opportunity to thank the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) for creating the IOU program used by the federal Government to build provincial court-houses. There are at least nine other

March 16, 1987
Oral Questions
communities in Ontario which have a need similar to that of the riding of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. I am sure they would like to participate in the IOU program of the Minister of National Revenue as well.
Mr. Speaker, I may be naive-
Hear, hear!
Oh, oh!

-but I came to the House of Commons this morning expecting to hear from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) about the Government's position on free trade. I suppose it is appropriate that his statement comes on the eve of St. Paddy's Day because what we got was more sham than we got at the Shamrock Summit. We got press releases, we got pronouncements, we got expostulations, but we got nothing from the mouth of the Prime Minister to let us know what I can tell the steel workers in my riding.
Is the Auto Pact on the table? Is agricultural policy on the table? What happens with the steel industry? What we got from the Government was more of obfuscation and mysterymaking. If the Prime Minister is serious about expecting to lead the country, he has the obligation to present his ideas and options here in the House of Commons as the Liberal Party has done. One of the reasons we have implicated the provinces and the First Ministers so deeply in the consultative process is, as one of them mentioned after Wednesday night's meeting, being so intimately involved in the process precludes any requirement for any ratification.

Bilateral Trade

speakeroldname: Hon. Pat Carney (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a rare privilege to have the opportunity to introduce a motion in the House which has the potential to enhance profoundly the future of our country, and that is my privilege today.
The trade debate is about Canada's future. It is about jobs-20th century jobs and 21st century jobs. It is about economic growth for those regions of Canada which are not sharing in the wealth that our present economic system provides. It is about sovereignty, because only an economically strong country can provide our unique social programs and preserve our cultural policies which protect our national identity. However, most of all, the great debate is about security and enhancing our access to our largest market and our biggest customer, the United States, in a long-term binding treaty.
This concept frightens some Canadians. It scares the opposition Parties which have no vision for Canada and offer no hope for Canadians who are unemployed now or who fear that they will be unemployed in the future as technology changes the nature of their jobs. Scare tactics are a cop-out. They are a way of browbeating Canadians back into the 19th century.
Our Government is prepared to lead Canadians through the final decade of the 20th century, turbulent with change, and into the 21st century, only 13 years away. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has said, we choose to negotiate not because it is easy and not because it is without political risk but because it is in our national interest. We serve that national interest, he reminds us, by securing an agreement with our largest trading partner which will provide stability and security for traders, investors, workers and for our future. Let me tell the House why this is so.
From the earliest days of mankind, from the era of barter systems through to the development of the first great trade routes, trade has been the generator of growth. Cities sprang up where traders met to exchange goods and all the world's great cities have their origins in trade. History is dominated by trade wars and their impact on the development and decline of regions. Trade has determined the future of nations and trade will determine the future of Canada.
Canada's economy is dependent on trade to a greater degree than almost any other country. Today we export about one-third of all we produce and we import about 30 per cent of what we consume. Growth in trade translates into growth in economic wealth. For the first 40 years since the post-war world first adopted the international rules of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, Canada's exports have multiplied 10 times over and our national wealth has more than tripled. Today our international trading system which helped create unprecedented wealth is in trouble. It is being

March 16, 1987
Bilateral Trade
eroded by protectionism as countries try to reduce unemployment by putting up barriers to other countries' goods and services.
Part of the problem is the GATT itself. Its institutions have become dated, its procedures are ineffective and its dispute mechanisms are often cumbersome. That is why the 92 countries of GATT met in Uruguay last fall to start the eighth round of trade liberalization under the GATT which was first established in 1947. One major objective of that round was to reduce trade barriers and to define rules and regulations for those areas in which no rules exist: areas like services, the fastest growing trade area, and intellectual property and investment. Very importantly, the agricultural sector has never been adequately covered by international rules and regulations.
If one wonders about the value of international rules and regulations governing trade, one need only take a look at the agricultural sector in which no such rules exist. The result is anarchy in agriculture. World agriculture trade is governed not by comparative advantage but by the size of national treasuries. For example, for every dollar the Japanese farmer receives, the Japanese taxpayer pays $2.50. For every dollar the European farmer receives, the European taxpayer pays $1.50. In the United States, the taxpayer pays $1.38 for each dollar the U.S. farmer receives. Canada cannot afford to compete with these huge subsidies and that is why the Prime Minister pushed so hard to get agriculture on the agenda of the economic summit.
Where does the U.S.-Canada bilateral fit into this worldwide picture? There are two answers. The first is jobs. We believe that this provides the best opportunity to create hundreds of thousands of new jobs and economic studies support this. I can cite studies done by the Economic Council of Canada which show that with free trade, as many as 370,000 jobs could be created in the next five years while we could lose half a million without free trade. University of Maryland studies indicated that a free trade agreement with the U.S. could cause an increase in the GPD of Canada of about 5 per cent. Trade is where the jobs are.
Second, we must deal with the rise in U.S. protectionism in a way that protects Canadian interests. As Atlantic fishermen, Quebec aerospace workers, Ontario steel workers, prairie farmers and British Columbia woodworkers know, we must trade to survive let alone to prosper and we are now fighting the ugliest outbreak of protectionism in the U.S. and around the world since the 1930s. We are fighting for those three million Canadians holding a quarter of Canadian jobs whose pay cheques depend on trade. We are fighting for a secure future and for more jobs in the years ahead.
American Congressmen and politicians are concerned about their trade deficit. For the first time in their memory, Americans are buying more from abroad than they are selling and they are losing jobs to overseas competition. They are turning inward, turning away from what gave them the strongest economy and the highest standard of living in the world. They
are using all sorts of weapons at their disposal, raising all kinds of non-tariff barriers to stop imports in the mistaken belief they can maintain jobs through protectionism.
In the last seven years, Americans have launched some 40 actions against Canadian goods. Many have failed but those that have succeeded have penalized Canadian exports worth over $6.5 billion. No region of Canada has remained untouched by American trade actions against us. These actions have cost Canadians opportunities and jobs.
There are no signs of weakening in the protectionist mood. There are hundreds of protectionist Bills awaiting action in the Congress. That mood should convince even the most skeptical Canadians that our trading relationship with the Americans is under attack. The new trade Bill would resume that attack if we are unsuccessful in our trade negotiations.
Let me deal with the agenda of the trade talks. We were asked this morning to specify the agenda. We have done so before but we are more than willing to do so again. First let me stress what is not on the table. Regional development and our capacity to sustain regional development is not on the table. Only the opposition Parties are dragging it onto the table. Our cultural policies and our ability to protect our national identity is not on the table. The negotiators know that that is not a subject for negotiation. Only the opposition Parties keep dragging it onto the table. Our social programs are not on the table. Again, only the opposition Parties raise our social programs and try to drag them onto the negotiating table. They are trying to put culture, regional development and social programs on the table, we are not.
Our negotiators are meeting today. Therefore, it is not in their interests to mention specific negotiating positions. However, I do want to say what is on the table and why we are dealing with these matters. Tariffs are on the table because experience has shown that the Canadian economy has prospered through tariff reduction. This is so even with the Auto Pact which the Opposition keeps bringing up. Members of the Opposition fail to mention that tariffs have come down steadily within the Auto Pact. For vehicles, they have come down from around 17.5 per cent to around 9.2 per cent. For auto parts, they have come down from as high as 25 per cent to 9.2 per cent. We have been reducing tariffs for years, and in the trade talks we are seeking to reduce them to zero on Canada-U.S. trade over a period of 10 or 15 years, whatever is negotiated.
Non-tariff barriers are on the table. Since the early 1970s, non-tariff barriers to trade have proliferated. Some are clear, imposing quotas on imports, for example. Some are not so clear, using technical or health standards for protectionism rather than for legitimate purposes. Another item on the table is government procurement practices. We are seeking to drop our "Buy Canadian" for their "Buy American", and as the Prime Minister pointed out today, 1 per cent of American government procurement could create 75,000 jobs in Canada.
March 16, 1987

Also on the table are customs matters. We want to facilitate commerce between the two countries by reducing the paperwork at the border. That will mean lower costs for Canadian businessmen. Agriculture is also on the table. I have touched upon the massive global problems we face in agriculture and they exist because there has been insufficient progress in bringing international rules to agricultural trade.
We know that we cannot resolve all our trading problems in the U.S.-Canada bilateral, but we can deal with some of them. We can deal with some tariffs, we can deal with health standards and we can deal with dispute settlement mechanisms that are used to harass agricultural products. Agriculture is very much a part of these talks.
Also on the table are subsidies and related measures. Those are important to regional development because under the existing trade laws, we often do not know what kind of subsidies we can use in regional development plans without bringing on U.S. trade actions. We want clear rules. We want to know what programs we will be able to implement for regional development. The existing international rules are not well defined and the U.S. is seeking to broaden them in, for example, the softwood lumber dispute and natural resource pricing. We want better rules in both countries because the U.S. subsidizes its products as well. We want better rules on what we can and cannot do. We need adjustment programs for the retraining which the Opposition talked about. We need programs for women.
One of the most important things on our agenda for negotiation are dispute settlement mechanisms. We want to replace the existing ones. The ones we have in place currently operate within the GATT framework but they do not make sense in application and they are unilateral. We want impartial mechanisms. For example, if the U.S. alleges that our stumpage programs are subsidies, we want an impartial, binational tribunal to deal with the issue, not the U.S. Department of Commerce.
Also on the table is intellectual property. This involves two issues: ensuring adequate protection for those who create new products, services or ideas, and ensuring access to those new products, services or ideas. Let me give you an example. One reason why companies locate their R and D in the U.S. is that if they want U.S. patent protection and someone else is developing the same idea, in the case of a tie the company which did its R and D in the U.S. gets preferred status. We do not like that because companies will locate in the U.S. to ensure their patents get U.S. patent protection. That means that good jobs for highly-trained Canadians are in doubt. We want free trade in intellectual property. We want free trade in services. This is a new area not now covered by international rules. More and more of our economy is service-based. It is about 67 per cent of our GPD these days. We have a solid record of growth in services of about 3 per cent per year. GATT is addressing these problems and new rules for services.
Bilateral Trade
So are we in the Canada-U.S. bilateral negotiations. We have some of the finest service industries in the world in engineering, financial consulting, computer services and banking. We are world-class competitors and we want to ensure access to world trade and services.
Also on the table is investment. All countries around the world are loosening their investment policies. We did so when FIRA became Investment Canada. The result was a record $6.8 billion worth of investment for 1986. So far we are dealing only with trade-related investment measures. The Americans want more. We are listening but we have not given the negotiators a general investment mandate.
The Opposition has raised the question of what the Americans want from this. Why are they bothering with the bilateral negotiations with Canada? What motivates them? Several things. First, we are their biggest market and their only growing market in the world today. Second, they want better rules on trade in goods and services and tariff procurement practices and provincial practices on intellectual property. They have the same agenda as we do. Much of this is new ground. What is very important to them is the trade and services agreement with us. The Americans can no longer dominate traditional markets such as steel and automobiles, and they threatened to walk away from GATT if trade and services was not included. The feeling in America is very strong that if they cannot make a deal with Canada in these new areas in particular, if they cannot define rules and regulations for new issues like services and intellectual property, they are unlikely to do it in the wider world of the GATT. They have a major and fundamental interest, even a historic interest, in trying to come to terms with us. So the conditions for these negotiations are far more balanced than the Opposition would lead us to believe.
We cannot stand still. Either we see our trading opportunities and eventually our prosperity fall prey to American protectionism, or we seek an agreement with Washington which will give us more secure access to that market. Let there be no doubt, standing still will make us poorer. Only moving forward will make us richer.
Hear, hear!

As Minister for International Trade no one knows better than I about the effect American trade remedy laws have had on our exports. We have seen it in shakes and shingles, fish, lumber, and farm products. Those unilateral decisions on what they call unfair practices are the problem between us. Americans call them fair trade laws but they are not. Americans say they cannot accept dumped or subsidized imports from us. We agree. We do not want theirs either. However, we do need a better way to work out these problems. If things were working smoothly neither side would need a change. The simple fact is that the present laws are not working and we need a way which eliminates the problems rather than introducing new barriers at the border. We need a system to ensure that neither country is penalized without a

March 16, 1987
Bilateral Trade
fair and impartial method of resolving disputes under agreed rules.
Let me repeat the message that the Prime Minister gave so clearly to this House. There will be no agreement without such a change. No agreement this Government signs will hold Canadian workers or industries hostage to the unpredictable whims of American protectionism. Canadians want to compete openly in a larger market with clear rules and fair access and that is the kind of agreement we are pursuing. For those who doubt what a trade deal with the United States can do they need look no further than the booming economy of southcentral Ontario. Much of that boom is based on what now amounts to free trade in automobiles. My colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), will be speaking more specifically about the Auto Pact a little later in this debate. Just let me remind Members of this House that there was considerable controversy over that agreement when it was negotiated more than 20 years ago. The Leader of the NDP in this House has consistently called for its renegotiation. Instead, it has been a resounding success and created thousands of jobs in Ontario. Those of us from other parts of the country watch this trade-based boom in Ontario with some envy. However, we mostly ask why our workers and our industries cannot have the same chance. If free trade is good for Ontario, why not for Atlantic Canada, Quebec, the Prairies, or British Columbia? What better way is there to reduce regional disparities than to give others a shot at competing in the American market on the same terms?
This Government has laid out what it is seeking to achieve, and why, in these negotiations with the U.S. We are seeking a secure economic future for Canadians working now and for those to come. We firmly believe that free trade is the best route to that goal. We have a plan and we are on track, but what do we hear from the other side of the House? From the Liberals we have a long complicated resolution which says "maybe", "if', "but", and "ifsoever". There is nothing positive in this long complicated Liberal amendment. There is no suggestion that there are other things which are equally important for us. There is the implication that if they do not get everything here in this long list, then maybe they do not want to proceed at all. I do not think that is good enough for Canadians.
From the NDP we have a long complicated motion presented at their convention this past weekend which says no to free trade. It says categorically: "Therefore be it resolved the New Democrats in Government will withdraw from the comprehensive trade negotiations presently taking place with the U.S. and would instead pursue the following trade strategy". It is a mishmash, a cherry-picking list of sectoral free trade. History has shown that sectoral free trade is not on for either country. It is not acceptable.
The NDP talk about GATT but ignores the fact that our negotiations are consistent with GATT. The Liberals make a point of saying they do not want an all-inclusive free trade agreement with the U.S. but they do want more negotiations in
GATT. Those two positions, as the Hon. Member knows, are inconsistent. You cannot have a free trade agreement consistent with GATT unless it is a comprehensive agreement. GATT will not permit it. The way we are going is the way we can go within GATT. The way the Liberals are pursuing this issue is inconsistent with the GATT that they talk so much about supporting.
I want to comment on one issue which is not sufficiently stressed in this House.

In closing, I want to speak about Canadians being world-class competitors, although the Opposition implies this is not the case. Canadians are not afraid of the future. The welders who are helping to build the oil pumping systems for Venezuela's oilfields at Canadian Foremost in Calgary know that they are as good as any in the world. They know, as we do, that we cannot deal with protectionism and prepare Canada for the next century if we walk away from this challenge.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am disappointed that the Hon. Member has found our report to Parliament to be so generalized. I thought I went into great detail to tell him what was on the agenda, what we were discussing, why we were discussing it, and why it is in our interest. That he thinks that, with Ambassador Murphy sitting at the negotiating table in this city, I would candidly chat about what our cards were and what cards we were playing today shows how ignorant he is of this historic negotiation. Hear, hear!

The Hon. Member raised the issue of safeguards. I want to assure him that the automobile industry in this country is working well above the level of safeguards. If production ever fell to the safeguards in the Auto Pact this country, the Province of Ontario, and that Member would be in trouble.
Finally, with regard to marketing boards we have said repeatedly that marketing boards are not the subject of negotiations. As my colleague, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), has patiently and repeatedly explained, and as is reflected in our resolution today, marketing boards are not a subject of these negotiations. Since I cannot put it more clearly than that, possibly the Member will wait until the Minister of Agriculture speaks on the issue.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister is aware of the threat to our steel exports from pending legislation in Congress. Could she review for us where our steel industry would stand should we conclude a free trade agreement with the United States? Specifically, what is the state of our industry? Can our industry continue to compete in that market, and are we fair traders?

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to respond to Mr. Steel who knows the answers to those questions far better than I do since he is one of my chief advisers on the steel issue. Yes, we are fair traders. Yes, we can compete in the U.S. Our problem is that we are taking a greater share of their markets than the Americans would like us to. That is precisely the kind of issue we want to address in these free trade negotiations.

I appreciate the Hon. Member's concern, but this again gets into the details of negotiations which are not appropriate for discussion at this time. We are discussing the over-all agenda and the areas in which we are seeking these kinds of agreements. I do not feel that it is useful at this point
