speechtext: The Hon. Member for Argenteuil- Papineau (Mrs. Bourgault) for a question or comment.

Mr. Speaker, Madam Minister, when I go back to my riding, I keep being asked by several of my constituents about the Canada-US relations, especially with regard to the triangle that involves Japan. Could the Minister explain the medium-and long-term benefits for Canada of a bilateral agreement with the United States as concerns our relations with Japan, for instance, which did not invest enough in Canada because our access to the American market was uncertain? Could the Minister tell me, or explain to my constituents what an agreement with the United States could mean to us by reason of the triangle with our second trade partner, Japan?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member raises an important point and she is entirely correct. Foreign investment in Canada means jobs. Our investment has historically been less than it could be because of uncertainty of access to the U.S. market. As long as we have the present countervail system and the present trade remedy laws, as long as there is great uncertainty about what we can and cannot do in order to access that market, it will be a drag on investments. All of my discussions with Japanese investors and the Japanese Government encourage me to believe that should we have security of access to the U.S. market and give the U.S. equal access to our market, that would be an access secured by a long-term, binding treaty. Foreign investment from Japan and other places would flow in increasing quantities to Canada and create jobs.

Mr. Speaker, I, too, welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate. It is two years late in terms of timing. The musty quality of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) speech which we heard this morning reflects the fact that it was drawn out of the vault, rather than being a contemporary analysis of the important issues and concerns facing Canada. Nevertheless, this is an opportunity for us to examine the anxiety as well as the opportunity Canadians expect from any trade strategy. First, I want to reiterate an important point made by the Leader of our Party this morning. The Liberals believe in expanding trade. Liberal Governments have been the most important architect of developing an international trade system. It was Liberal Governments that helped develop the GATT, that moved the trading realm into the broad reach around the world.
It was Liberal Governments that negotiated the Auto Pact which the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) said was one of the important elements of present day progress.

March 16, 1987
Bilateral Trade
May I remind her that the negotiation of the Auto Pact had nothing to do with the kind of trade the Government is negotiating. It was a managed trade agreement with guarantees on both sides of the border about jobs, investment, and content. Any attempt to try to sell the Auto Pact as being the model the Government is following is another example of the maladroitness of the Government to try again to raise a smokescreen rather than deal with facts. Therefore, we take no backseat in terms of a commitment to expanding the horizons of international trade opportunities.
At the same time, I believe the peculiar genius of Canadian trade policies since the Second World War until this Government has been the recognition that while one must expand that trade it must be done both by strengthening international rules so that big, middle and small countries were equally protected and building up our own distinctive institutions at home to preserve our identity as a country and preserve the right to make our own economic decisions in Canada. It is necessary to preserve our right to make choices in order to maintain that important balance in sharing the North American continent with one of the largest and most powerful countries in the world. That has served us well until now.
The Government has deliberately veered from that course and made a major shift in the basic Canadian understanding that we must expand trade but not sacrifice our rights and freedoms to make choices about ourselves, our institutions and our economic programs. That is the cause we are raising today: how to adopt a trade strategy that expands trade but does not sacrifice the very basic elements of sovereignty in this country and the right to make economic choices for ourselves.
Let us examine what has been said today. The Minister, the Prime Minister and, I suppose, the resolution allude to some kind of commitment to this international trade system. However, the Government has cut back the number of embassies and consulates. It has cut back funds for the Export Development Corporation. It has downgraded the place of the ambassador for multilateral trade so that she plays second fiddle to the Canada-U.S. negotiators when the opposite should be true.
All the Government's actions have been designed to restrict our capacity to broaden our trade base. Perhaps the clearest example is in the Prime Minister's comments this morning about his objectives. He said he is trying to achieve a special deal for Canada, that there are a lot of unfair traders in the world whom the Americans do not like but since Canadians are fair we will negotiate a special deal for ourselves. Is that the way to reinforce and strengthen the international trade system? Is that the way to provide a proper balance of interest to ensure that there are rules that apply to large and small alike? Is the Prime Minister not really abandoning the Canadian tradition and the interests we have tried to pursue in strengthening that international system?
The Government has contradicted its objectives by its actions. We hear the rhetoric, but when it comes to action we see that the Government is not interested in multilateral trade
or expanding its international options. It is preoccupied with getting this kind of trade arrangement with the Americans which carries with it very serious implications for this country.
The Government says that the reason it wants this agreement is to create jobs. No one will object to creating more jobs, but where is the proof that more jobs will be created?
The Government refers to the Macdonald Royal Commission. Unfortunately, the figures it used were out of date and did not take into account the reduction in tariffs that had occurred under the GATT system. The Macdonald Commission devoted all of three paragraphs to the surface industries which generate some 60 per cent to 70 per cent of new jobs in this country. There is no research or examination, just three paragraphs outlining the job impact on the surface industries.
What proof does the Prime Minister have for stating that a flourish of regional development will result from this proposed trade deal? There was certainly nothing in the paper the Government tabled several months ago to prove that. Yet I can refer to the study by the Canada West Foundation which generally purports to support free trade but says jobs will be lost in western Canada in food processing, in furniture making, in the service industries, in the horticultural industries, in poultry and in dairy industries. Do we hear the Prime Minister say there will be a loss of jobs in the balance? No. While certainly there will be some benefits, there will also be losses but there is absolutely no recognition of it. The study "l'actua-lite" in the Province of Quebec revealed that 280,000 jobs in the Province of Quebec alone were in jeopardy. There is the Radwanski study for the Government of Ontario which indicated that hundreds of thousands of jobs in the service industry were at risk.
The fact is that there is no clear evidence that an incredible bonanza is being created.
It is useful to refer to a study commissioned by the Province of Manitoba. It states:
For the sake of discussion, let us assume that free trade with the U.S. will now generate a further five per cent increase in real GNP. Since any liberalization of trade would be phased in over ten years, we could only expect GNP to increase each year by about half a percentage point more than would be the case if we maintained the status quo. Given that, over the past ten years, the average amount by which real growth rates varied from year to year was 3.4 percentage points, there is no way we will notice whether or not we have obtained our extra half a point of growth or not. In other words, we may never even notice the benefits of free trade, even if they do occur.
It is worth considering whether the problems associated with free trade will be equally invisible.
The fact is that when we consider all the evidence, all the computer print-outs from the high-priced economic think tanks, do we really have the kind of guarantee of the bonanza we hear about from the Prime Minister or the Minister for International Trade? There is absolutely no such assurance. In fact, we must begin to ask how many more jobs will be at risk and what will be the results if we do not provide the adjustment programs that our Leader talked about this morning to at least insure there is some kind of cushion.
March 16, 1987

If the Minister for International Trade is so smart, she will vote for our amendment. She will support our amendment because it includes the kinds of requirements we believe are important, such as a major adjustment program. The Government forgot to include such programs in its motion. It will let everyone hang in the wash, and all those workers who are affected can go on the scrap heap, as far as the Government is concerned.
The Government can show that this is not its policy by supporting a Liberal trade policy. We have the experience to show what must be done in this country to provide a rational approach. The Minister accused the Opposition of engaging in scare tactics, but she does not understand. We are not frightened of expanding trade, we are frightened of the Government's approach to it. We are frightened of a Minister who negotiates a deal on softwood lumber that imposes a 15 per cent tariff on our industry, throws the secondary manufacturing industry in to sweeten the pot somehow by accident, and agrees to increase stumpage fees, building in another $300 million or $400 million. She does not take into account the exchange rate so we will have higher costs. This is a Minister who says: "Trust us". This is a Minister who has probably committed one of the great all time give-away sell-outs in the history of trade and she says: "Have confidence in me. I am going to do a great job". What earthly reason can we have, after the debacle of the softwood trade issue, to have any confidence in this Minister or this Government? Can the Government explain why we should trust it when we see what it has already done in the cultural industries? It tells us that culture is not at stake, but it gave away Prentice Hall. It tells us not to worry about industry, but it gave away our patent production. Every time we turn around the Government is negotiating on its knees once again, yet it says: "Don't worry about it. We will do it okay next time".
The reason we raised in our amendment the kinds of very clear conditions we did is that Canadians are equally afraid of what the Government has done. They know full well, whether they are farmers in southwestern Ontario or in the interior of British Columbia that they are at risk when it comes to negotiating the supply systems and the export and import controls. The Minister says: "I am going to bring down tariffs". Does that mean the Government is going to negotiate the seasonal tariffs? Does it mean the Minister is going to put the farmers in Ontario and British Columbia, the farmers in the Fraser Valley and large parts of southern Ontario and New Brunswick out of business? That is the implication of her remarks. That is the clear message she is giving. That is what she is negotiating away if she is going to reduce those tariffs. Our Party kept them in there because we recognize the need to protect those industries.
What is it that the Government is trying to negotiate? The Minister began to give her own little shopping list, and that really begins to telegraph clearly why this debate should have happened much earlier. It should have happened at the time
Bilateral Trade
the report of the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons indicated that there should be a debate in the House of Commons first before we get into negotiation. The former chairman is here and will know that I certainly supported that recommendation. The fact is that what really is at stake is that level playing field about which the Americans like to talk. It is the idea that we are going to negotiate away our right to choose for ourselves what subsidies or programs we will be able to apply domestically to support our own industries. The Minister has conceded that this is on the table. She has said that we are going to negotiate subsidies, services and investment. We now know that the Government is engaged at the present time in negotiating away the kind of independence Canada will require in order to initiate and control its own economic formula.
1 would like to refer for a moment to a Manitoba study done by a Dutch economist, Goran Therborn, on the 15 OECD countries. He analysed them from the point of view of which countries have succeeded in gaining full employment and those which had the worst record. When one takes those 15 countries and analyses the factors, one asks oneself, is it related to export performance? No. Is it even related to economic growth figures? No, it is not. What Mr. Therborn analyses is that the primary rationale, if one compares the top five countries and the bottom five countries in the OECD, and their capacity for creating employment, was the capacity to have an independent economic decision-making so they could choose the kind of policies and programs they need when they need them. That is exactly what the Government is negotiating away. It is exactly what is on the table. The kinds of rights the Government is abandoning is the right of the Government to be able to select the mixture of programs we can apply as a country to secure more employment for Canadians. That is the kind of analysis which should have been done by the Government, but it was never done. That is one reason we believe it is very important to establish those kinds of conditions and requirements to ensure we preserve the right to choose what subsidies we apply for high technology development, what kind of support programs we have in the area of regional development, to ensure the Government does not negotiate Bill C-58, another service industry, to ensure we do not abandon the kind of guarantees we have in telecommunications, trucking and other service industries which provide a large percentage of our jobs. But we now have the admission that that is what is being negotiated away. That is what is on the table.
I would say to the Conservatives opposite that if they want to provide confidence that in fact they will not negotiate away those rights, because they say that somehow we are putting up a screen, then they have one very clear way of proving it. They can vote for our amendment. They can give us right now in this House all the assurance and guarantees which Canadians need, but I do not think they are going to do it. They will not give those assurances because that is what they are negotiating away.

March 16, 1987
Bilateral Trade
The Government tries to pretend that this is the only alternative, that the only way we can have a dispute settlement mechanism is through a bilateral agreement. It tells us that the only way we can deal with countervail powers is through a bilateral agreement. Of course, that is not true. The fact is there are already in place perfectly good mechanisms under the GATT system for dealing with those issues.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: They don't work.

The Parliamentary Secretary says they will not work. We know the level of understanding he has about trade matters. Canada has already taken seven matters to the GATT and has had five decided in its favour. We have already used an impartial panel to determine what is right or wrong. The Minister tells us we are going to get an impartial panel of Canadians and Americans to decide this. If we really want an independent panel, Mr. Speaker, perhaps we should have an impartial panel of people who do not have any vested interest in the issue at all.
We also know full well that we could have within the existing system of GATT other kinds of applications to offset the matter. However, the one time the Government had the opportunity to prove that it believed in the international system, to prove we could make the system work, it backed away. In fact, it foreclosed the right of Canada to go to GATT on the softwood lumber case. We signed it away as part of the agreement. We did not even have the guts or courage to pursue that issue. We signed it away. Do not think, Mr. Speaker, that that does not set a precedent. Do not think that many other countries around the world are not seeing how Canada is putting its tail between its legs and running for cover. That does not contribute to the enhancement and growth of the international trade system.
It is true that the world is heading towards the emergence of regional blocks. There is no question that that is one of the clear and prevailing dangers in world trade. However, is it the solution or antidote for us to join the pack? Is it our solution to try to push that trend along as opposed to offsetting it? Should we not be fighting against that trend and showing we have a different solution?
We know, of course, and it is clear, that one has to continue dealing with the Americans. We have made many deals in the past as a Liberal Government. In fact, one of the last successful commercial arrangements signed was when I negotiated in the transportation area back in 1984. It was certainly more successful than anything the Minister for International Trade has been able to sign until now. Of course, we know we have to continue talking, discussing and negotiating. But we should make it very clear that the attempt to provide for the wide open, unrestricted, all inclusive ambition which will incorporate the concept of national treatment and prevent us from maintaining our capacity and ability to decide for ourselves what kind of economic blueprint we want for Canada, is what is really at stake.
That is why the amendment we put forward clearly recognizes the need to support the international system, to avoid the kind of entanglements an all-inclusive trade agreement would provide, and that any negotiations should seek to preserve the rights of Canadians to maintain their freedom of choice. That is the basis of our trade policy. It is far more clear, cogent and effective than anything we have received in the kind of resolution the Tories put forward today. That is why we think Canadians are turning against the Government. They do not have trust or confidence that it can negotiate well or is negotiating towards the right objectives.

Mr. Speaker, I have three questions I would like to put to the Hon. Member. First, if the softwood settlement was so devastating to the industry, as the Hon. Member and his Leader suggest, could he explain to me why the stocks of MacMillan Bloedel have gone up 100 per cent since December 29, the day before our settlement, which is leading to the first stock split since the two companies were merged in 1959? Can the Hon. Member explain this 100 per cent increase in the stock of MacMillan Bloedel and the 127 per cent increase in the stock of Canfor?
Second, can the Hon. Member explain why he would have preferred $600 million going to the U.S. Treasury under the countervail when, under our settlement, that money will stay in Canada?
With respect to the GATT, the Hon. Member's Party was opposed to the duties on books which were imposed in response to the shakes and shingles issue. Can the Hon. Member explain how, if we had won before the GATT, therefore winning the right to seek compensation in the form of other duties against American goods, he would have imposed $600 million worth of duties on American goods coming into Canada which would have hurt our competitive position?

Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that the Minister has not taken the time to read the proceedings of the committee which has been examining Bill C-37. If she had she would have had her questions answered for her. In light of the fact that she has not taken the time to read the transcripts of the testimony, I can relate to her the type of evidence that has been given. Perhaps it will stimulate her into actually examining the issues at hand.
With respect to the softwood lumber settlement itself, the Minister says that the stock market is now the arbiter with respect to whether this is a good deal or a bad deal. She seems to think that the stock market will indicate whether there is a healthy economy or not. What has been pointed out is that the burst in the price of MacMillan Bloedel stocks was due to the progress being made in the pulp and paper industry. Many of the companies dealing exclusively in softwood lumber are in fact being negatively affected at the present time. Between 80 and 100 companies have been forced to go out of business in the secondary remand areas.
March 16, 1987

Mike Apsey, who is the Executive Director of COFI and who appeared before us, said that the fact of the matter is that whatever boom is being experienced in the lumber industry is a result of the completion of inventories after the strike. As they head further into the third and fourth quarters they will face a downturn in the industry. The 15 per cent added cost differential means that the threshold of closing of mills and the threshold of losing money is so much higher than it was before that many of these companies have lost their flexibility. If the Minister thinks that good trade policy should be based on what goes up and down on the Toronto Stock Exchange from day to day, then I say that that is an awfully good reason why Canadians should have even less confidence today than they had yesterday in the capacity of the Minister for International Trade.
The Minister asks whether or not we would have liked to keep the $600 million here in Canada. We said all along that we had a good case. We were convinced that we could have won, in which case no one would have had to spend $600 million on anything. This is $600 million which has been imposed on the Canadian forest industry. It cuts the capacity to expand. It cuts the capacity for capital investment. It also raises the threshold of plant closures. The fact of the matter is we believe that the country could have successfully pursued the case through either the American tribunal or the GATT tribunal. We believe, as does the industry, that the case could have been won or that we could have had the tariff reduced.
It is ironic that this is a Government which says that the market-place is right, that we must listen to private enterprise, but if it comes down to a choice of obtaining the advice of the industry then the Government turns its substantial other cheek and says: "No. We will not listen to that advice".
With respect to going to the GATT, as our Leader said this morning we had already paid for access of our softwood lumber to the American market under the Tokyo round of negotiations. We had given very broad-based access to American goods in the computer business equipment area, which makes up close to a $10 billion market. That was part of the deal that was negotiated. The Americans broke the deal. We were an accomplice in the breaking of that deal by going along with it. The fact of the matter is that if we had been given the right to retaliate, if many American industries, the big multinationals-the IBMs and the Burroughs, which presently have open access to the Canadian market because of the softwood lumber case-had felt they would be restricted, there might have been a very different set of political pressures brought to bear in the United States.
Once again, that is the reason we need a Government that can think through a trade strategy and that does not simply react to some Pavlovian stimulus provided by the Premier of British Columbia whose last job was running Fantasy Land and whose next job may be doing the same thing. That is why we are arguing in our amendment for something that begins to make sense.
Bilateral Trade
I suggest that if the Minister wants further elaboration on these important points there are several hundred pages of transcript that might provide useful reading for her.

Mr. Speaker, like many Members of the House I have been studying this omnibus resolution. That is what we called it at our convention this weekend since it covers just about everything. I wish to ask my good friend, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), if this resolution were to pass would it indicate an acceptance of a comprehensive bilateral deal with the United States or would it indicate a rejection of such a comprehensive deal? I have trouble trying to sort this out, which may be my fault. I have trouble trying to sort out whether the conditions, if they were accepted, would be sufficient to put the Liberal Party solidly behind this initiative.

Mr. Speaker, I am always interested in helping the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) in trade matters and to give him the best advice I can to develop his understanding of these matters. With respect to the question he raised, there is a very easy and simple answer. The Hon. Member should read the first paragraph of our amendment in which we state that we oppose an all-inclusive trade arrangement with the United States. I do not think I can be much clearer than that.
In listening to the speech of the Hon. Member's Leader this afternoon I heard him say that members of his Party are not against negotiating with the Americans but that they have certain conditions as well. That sounds to me as if the NDP is about ready to support the Liberal amendment. Considering the events of last week, I think that would be only fair under the circumstances.
The amendment speaks for itself. We oppose an all-inclusive agreement which would set out a whole series of conditions which we feel must guide any other form of negotiation or agreement that is being made. We welcome the support of the New Democratic Party in this regard, just as we welcome the support of the Conservatives in the establishment of a clear trade policy.

Mr. Speaker, I take exception to the remarks of the Hon. Member with respect to the Premier of British Columbia, who we feel is doing an excellent job on behalf of British Columbia. I am sure that the Leader of the Hon. Member's Party would want to dissociate himself from the comments of the Hon. Member. It would not be the first or the last time, I am sure, that the two do not agree.
Speakers this morning have cited many quotations. I would like to add to those which have been put forward this morning and read the following:
Yielding to protectionism under the guise of economic nationalism is self-defeating for Canada. This country has always proposed freer rules of international trade. Ad hoc retaliation here and there is not ultimately in the Canadian interest. If any of the current reciprocity Bills before the U.S. Congress ever become law, Canadians will learn what retaliation is all about.

March 16, 1987
Business of the House
I am sure Hon. Members think that perhaps those are the words of one of our Ministers or a member from this side of the House. In fact, it is a statement made by the Hon. Member's Leader back in 1982 when he was with McMillan Binch. I applaud the comments of the Leader of the Opposition. I think he takes the right approach, an open approach to free trade.
Can the Hon. Member advise me how he can reconcile the views of his Leader, which were so forcefully and appropriately set out in 1982, and the view which he has just stated that his Party is against an all-inclusive trade arrangement with the United States? The amendment which has been put forward contains so many caveats and so many ifs, ands and buts, it is like sending a boxer into the ring with both hands tied. How can one negotiate an arrangement with all that? In fact, it reminds me of a cross between a horse and a donkey. We all know what that would end up with. It would be a mule that is sterile and cannot produce. With this type of amendment the Liberal Party will not be producing either. Would the Hon. Member care to enlighten me on the discrepancy between his Leader and himself with respect to this particular issue?

Mr. Speaker, first let me say to the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) that in referring to the Premier of British Columbia I was simply stating a fact that that was his last place of employment. If the Hon. Member is disputing that, then it is only consistent with the Tories inability to deal with facts and reality by always dealing in the realm of fiction. The hon. gentleman is now the Premier of British Columbia and, of course, we will accord all the honour due that position. We will listen to him with interest as he makes statements or ruminates on matters of trade or other such matters.
I want to come to the main part of the member's question about the ability to have retaliation. There is a major difference. Ad hoc retaliation is what the Government used on the shakes and shingles. It brought in a sort of stupid tax on books that simply crippled the book industry, to say nothing of having deprived widows of their tea and children of their Christmas trees. That is what you call an ad hoc capricious, silly retaliation.
And the Minister finally recognized it.

The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), who is usually nine months behind time, recognized his error by bringing in a correction to his Budget.
I was talking about a clearly determined right of retaliation under international rules. Where there is a major countervail action, as the United States took on softwood lumber which we consider to be totally unfair, given redress by GATT under the international rules we would have been able to apply a proper mode of retaliation under those rules. That is what makes those rules work, and that is the point we are after. Let us
make the rules work. Let us have an international system that works effectively instead of skirting around it, trying to get out from under all the time, which has been the practice of the Conservative Government. We believe that if the system worked properly, and we think it would have worked properly-the Americans themselves say their interest is in broadening international rules-we would not have had to retaliate. The Americans would have backed down on the countervail and we would not have $600 million being applied against our lumber industry today.

Mr. Speaker, after listening to the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) presentation today and hearing his presentation indicating a willingness to discuss the whole matter of the negotiated settlement prior to the final decision with Parliament, we concur that the debate take place into the evening and the vote be held tomorrow at 6 p.m.

Motion agreed to.
March 16, 1987

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Miss Carney:
That this House supports the negotiation of a bilateral trading arrangement with the United States, as part of the government's multilateral trade policy, while protecting our political sovereignty, social programs, agricultural marketing systems, the auto industry, and our unique cultural identity.
And on the amendment of Mr. Turner (Vancouver Quadra) (p. 4158):

Mr. Speaker, before 1 begin my remarks in this debate, I want to express my appreciation to my two colleagues, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) for allowing me to enter the debate at this time enabling me to fulfil a long time commitment with a large number of eastern Ontario farmers later tonight.
Canadian agriculture has an important stake in international trade negotiations. And, as Minister of Agriculture, I am pleased to speak for Canadian farmers in the Cabinet, in the House and on their behalf in the bilateral trade negotiations.
The federal Government understands and appreciates the importance of Canada's farm industry. Furthermore, we believe that the family farm is and should continue to be at the heart of the industry. Canadians, too, understand that agriculture touches all of our lives every day. We do not take for granted the contribution that our farm industry makes to the national economy and to the economies of many rural towns and villages from coast to coast. We do not take for granted the 1.6 jobs provided directly or indirectly by the agriculture and food industry. And certainly no Canadian should ever take for granted this country's reliable supply of high quality reasonably-priced food. Indeed, the Government's top priority commitment to agriculture is a commitment to a strong, healthy agri-food industry and thus a strong, healthy Canadian economy.
That is why our Government has undertaken many helpful and important agricultural initiatives. Most significantly, we delivered the SI billion special Canadian grains program, the largest special initiative ever taken on behalf of Canadian farmers by any federal Government in the history of Canada. This and many other actions are tangible proof that we have acted in good faith on behalf of farmers. In the same way we are acting in good faith and in the best interests of our farmers in our international trade negotiations.
Canada's farm industry truly reflects the trading heritage of this nation. Close to half of last year's farm cash receipts in Canada, about $9 billion, were derived from export sales alone. That is why it is essential we get the best possible deal for agriculture in our international trade negotiations.
Bilateral Trade
Let me speak first about the problems of international trade and grains. The ill-conceived export subsidy war between the treasuries of the EEC, and the U.S. is making victims of Canadian farmers. The Government of Canada is determined to see an end to this insane subsidy war. We are fighting for fairness in world agricultural trade. Most Canadian farmers understand and appreciate our many efforts. For example, Canada played a key role in having agriculture put on the table in the new round of multinational negotiations. We are now pursuing the Canadian interest with vigour at the GATT. At the Tokyo Summit last year, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Minister of Finance, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) expressed the need for an end to the international subsidy war as a matter of urgency.
I am positive the Prime Minister will be doing the same at the upcoming summit. My colleague, the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, has met twice to discuss grain trade problems with the five major grain exporting nations. Canada, in fact, initiated the first meeting. There will be more. We must find a solution. We must restore fairness and equity to the international trade world.
These multilateral initiatives do not stand alone. Canada is also acting on another important international front, namely, bilaterally, to improve our trading relationship with the United States. The Americans are by far Canada's largest export customer for farm products. When you realize that the United States is a relatively small customer for our major farm export, grains and oil seeds, then the significance of the U.S. market becomes even more obvious and apparent. More than half of our non-grain and oil seed farm exports are sold to the U.S. market. Sales of our farm products to the United States equalled 10 per cent of all farm cash receipts in Canada.
The importance of the United States market varies from one commodity to the next, but that is Canadian agriculture. It is an important point to remember. For instance, about three-quarters of our red meat exports go to the United States. Without exports to the Americans, our red meat industry would shrink dramatically. About two-thirds of our horticultural and special crops go to the United States, and well over half our potatoes are exported to the United States. In fact, if we look at the Canadian pork industry, we see that well over a third of all pork produced in Canada is sold in the U.S. market.
Clearly a strong future for many sectors of our farm industry is contingent upon future access to our largest market, namely, the U.S. This is why many farmers are, and rightfully should be, concerned about the increasing protectionist move which is running rampant south of the border.
We have all seen the writing on the wall. Action by U.S. pork producers resulted in the imposition of a countervail duty on live swine. A number of midwestern states restricted imports of our live animals and meats for more than a year. It was allegedly done for health reasons, but it was really to keep

March 16, 1987
Bilateral Trade
Canadian products out of the U.S. market. U.S. potato producers in Maine continue to try to restrict Canadian potato markets in that particular region. The legal costs of this action and the imposition of special inspection procedures create a hardship for potato producers in the country, particularly those in eastern Canada.
There were anti-dumping and countervail duty investigations into British Columbia raspberries. Restrictive import quotas were imposed on certain sugar products. This has caused an estimated trade loss to Canada of about $40 million. Now there is an investigation of beef imports from Canada.
Canadian farmers are not standing still during this process. Many farm groups are beginning to take successful action on their own to protect their own interests. Even as we negotiate nation to nation for new and better rules governing agricultural trade, we cannot and will not leave ourselves disarmed.
A good example is the corn countervail decision which was issued on March 6 by the Canadian Import Tribunal. It found that American subsidized corn was causing injury to Canada's grain corn industry. This decision was a direct result of farmers' own actions.
All these disputes point to the troubling changes which are taking place in our trading relationship with the United States. For our farmers these disputes create uncertainty about the future and future market opportunities. Unless there is an effort on both sides of the border to discuss and resolve these difficulties through the negotiation of a new trade deal, we can bet that there will be more problems and indeed more trade barriers.
The benefits for Canadian farmers will be tremendous, if we are able to negotiate a new trade deal with the United States. It must be a deal that prevents many disputes from happening in the first place. It must be a deal that establishes a reliable and fair mechanism for handling disputes which arise in a manner that does not involve new trade barriers. It must be a deal which, once and for all, regulates technical barriers in order to prevent their use to block trade, and a deal which gives Canada more secure access to our largest agricultural market.
From an agricultural standpoint, that is what these negotiations are all about. They are about fighting off the ground swell of protectionism in the United States, and they are about securing Canada's access to a large American market of some 235 million people.
To get the best deal possible, we are consulting fully with the industry, with all sectors, and with all provinces. I should like to make mention of the membership of Walter Kroeker and Ted Turner on the permanent International Trade Advisory Board. In addition, we have some 15 sectoral advisory groups on international trade. We also have one of the largest sectoral groups on agriculture, food, and beverages, with about 34 members.
More than half the total farm cash receipts in the country are derived from the sale of commodities covered by marketing boards. Producers of many commodities from grains to turkeys to hogs have been served well by the marketing board system. Today there are about 125 active marketing boards in Canada, and the vast majority of them are promotional in nature and established under provincial legislation.
However, an important distinction must be made for dairy, poultry, and egg farmers who operate under a full supply-management system. I appreciate the concern among some of these producers about what our negotiations with the United States may mean for them. My cabinet colleagues are well aware of those concerns as well.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney), and the Prime Minister have stated the Government's position on the issue very clearly. In fact, the motion before the House clearly addresses itself to that problem. I have repeated the message time and time again that the Government will retain the right to decide in Canada what kind of marketing systems are best for our agricultural commodities. We are not about to dismantle the Canadian Wheat Board or any other marketing boards, whether or not they have supply-management powers. Let me make that statement very clear. We are talking with the Americans about trade, but we will not sign any deal unless the deal is a good one for Canadian farmers. Obviously any deal which is a good deal for Canadian farmers is a good deal for Canadians generally.
The Government's position on agriculture in the trade negotiations reflects the high priority we place upon the country's agri-food industry. We believe that our positions, our policies, and our actions must and do reflect a commitment to a healthy and viable farm industry in Canada.
I welcome whatever time is remaining for questions.

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Minister to expand a little on what he is saying about marketing boards, in particular the Canadian Wheat Board and the grain commission. Mr. Yeutter, the U.S. Trade Commissioner, has stated very specifically that they cannot accept the grading system established in Canada and that it is unfair to them. In fact, he called it "phoney". That grading system has made us the producer of the best grains in the world, and the United States has complained about it for many years. It has suggested that it wants the system out of the way and that if we are to have a level playing field, it must be out of the way. I want the Minister to assure us that the Government respects the grading system which is in place as far as grains are concerned.

Mr. Speaker, I suppose I can take some satisfaction from the fact that at least the question is a different one. For the last six months or eight months certain people have been travelling around the country deliberately stirring up some uneasiness and anxiety by indicating "forget it, fellows, you are going to lose your marketing system". They have indicated to people who have operated so well under supply-
March 16, 1987

management-and some of them have done so for 50 years- that it will go down the tubes.
I hope we have established the facts very clearly today. When the Hon. Member started his question, I thought he was about to raise again a question about the possibility of the Canadian Wheat Board being dissolved or disappearing after the talks. The fact of the matter is that it will not be. We have deliberately used the term "agricultural marketing system". I indicated that we have about 125 boards in the country. Some of the boards have supply-management and some do not. Some are marketing commissions. Some are not much more than associations. Some are groups of producers who sit down on behalf of their membership to try to negotiate contracts with processors and so on. Maybe we are making progress here in respect of the Canadian Wheat Board.
I suppose the grading system is like any other grading system for a whole variety of products. We have some real problems with the grading systems in reference to our U.S. counterparts, and we would not mind talking about that at all. They have a habit of changing these things overnight without even giving us the courtesy of notifying us. They happen to use all sorts of things that give us problems, and I think that is one of the trade irritants about which we should talk.
I can tell the Hon. Member one thing and that is that we will not make any decision on changing the grading systems until such time as we fully utilize the advisory group that exists and until we touch base with the industry people. My colleague, the Minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board will, I am certain, be using each and every occasion to seek the advice of the leadership of the grain trade before we make any move on that particular aspect of it.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister's colleague, the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney), indicated earlier today that the Government would be seeking to reduce customs duties, to reduce tariffs and to negotiate in the area of investment and services. Taking that into account, I would like to ask the Minister some explicit questions.
If investment is to be negotiated, would that affect the way U.S. grain companies compete with prairie grain co-operatives and pools which now have special investment advantages? Second, if by negotiating import quotas and tariffs we allow for import restrictions on U.S. grain to be lifted, how will that affect the two-price wheat system? Third, if customs duties on imported fruits and vegetables are revoked or removed, would that not affect our emergency protection laws as well as our seasonal customs duties that now apply for the protection of the horticultural industry? Fourth, how would this affect the wineries in British Columbia and Ontario? The Minister for International Trade said that we would negotiate away government procurement. The wine and beer industries are based on the special advantages they now enjoy with liquor commissions across Canada. Have all those applications of the Government's plan been examined?
Bilateral Trade

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate those questions. In response to a question which I believe was posed by the Hon. Member's colleague, the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) earlier today, I made it very clear. When we make a clear statement dealing with agricultural marketing systems like the one we made in today's motion, there should be no doubt that we are sending a clear signal across the country that we will maintain the right to decide in Canada what system of marketing a particular commodity deems advisable for its own use. We are also recognizing the continuation of supply management.
Some marketing boards have supply management, but the Canadian Wheat Board is a little different. It does not have supply management powers but it does have powers to issue import permits. We have sent a clear signal that the Canadian Wheat Board stays and that marketing boards, even those with supply management powers, stay. At the same time, there must be a recognition that certain underpinnings are required and will have to remain in place. There is no way the supply management system can operate unless it continues to have other trade advantages.
Let us look at the dairy industry, for example. We can compare any dairy farm in Canada with a dairy farm in the State of Florida. The farmer in the State of Florida will probably not have any more money in his entire operation than the average dairy farmer in Canada has in his or her milk house. That is just common sense. Those who understand the industry know that there is no way Canadian dairymen could compete against dairymen south of the State of Georgia because of weather conditions alone. The same is true of the middle states. Any state further south of Georgia has two crops a year. How in the world can we compete against that? We must recognize that reality. We will not shut them down at all.
With reference to Sections 56 and 57 of the fruit, vegetable and honey regulations, again I indicated in answer to the Hon. Member's colleague that I have an option to express my views on that in accordance with the new rules of the House and I will do so. I will exercise my option on behalf of the Canadian fruit and vegetable industry on Wednesday, I believe. I hope that all Hon. Members, regardless of political affiliation, will join with me in support of that motion so those regulations are not rescinded.
I have spoken of geographic locations and the economy of scale. We always have to be conscious of those. We live in half of the North American continent. Americans can put 10 per cent of their produce into this market and occupy 100 per cent of it. We could put 100 per cent of our produce down there and it would only impact on about 10 per cent of the market. We know that. In fact, I have established a Canada-U.S. port advisory group which has worked well together and will continue working together. There is a respect for our need to pay special attention to those items which impact on Canadian agriculture and particularly the fruit and vegetable industry at certain seasons of the year.

March 16, 1987
Bilateral Trade
As I have travelled across the country, I have experienced some frustration. A member of my staff told me that I made 190 speeches last year, and I will probably make as many in the future if I have the good fortune to remain in this particular position. As I travel around the country, I find that almost without exception, people are pretty edgy on the trade issue, particularly those who work in supply-managed commodities. I acknowledge that. However, we have decided, and it is the right decision, that we should only say certain things at certain times. 1 know my colleague, the Minister for International Trade made that point today in answer to my colleague across the way. Whatever we do, we must not jeopardize our chances of striking the best possible deal. We have satisfied ourselves at this point in time that we can be very definite on marketing systems with supply management. The process will go on and as time goes by and negotiations continue, we will be making more definite statements on other aspects as well.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister a couple of questions about Canadian dairy farmers. Of course, the Minister probably has a copy of the letter that was addressed to him by the president of their association dated March 13. The dairy farmers made a number of points on the free trade deal with the United States as it relates to the dairy industry to which I would like the Minister to respond.
First, dairy farmers say that their domestic market must not become a disposal ground for U.S. overproduction. The Minister already stated that certain parts of the United States can certainly produce more cheaply than we can in Canada due to our geographic dislocation, if you will, and climatic conditions. This is what bothers the dairy industry, certainly in my province, about free trade. I am sure they would like to have some assurances from the Minister that the import control list is a fundamental element of the Canadian supply management system and it must not be weakened under any conditions in these negotiations. On the contrary, they say that if any changes are to be made they should go towards strengthening of the list, notably through the addition of dairy products such as yogurt and ice cream. If we do not have some way of stopping the import of those products, especially those in the dairy sector, given their longer production runs and their ability to compete against us, then supply management will be thrown out of the window as far as Atlantic Canadian farmers are concerned.

Mr. Speaker, I believe I dealt with that question earlier in Question Period and in my other remarks. This Government provided dairy farmers with a five-year commitment of $1.5 billion. This motion we are debating today indicates that supply management stays. The long-term dairy policy stays. There is no question about that. The Hon. Member should take some comfort from that. I also said that would require the retention of certain underpinnings now in place in order to maintain the commitment to that long-term dairy policy. Dairy farmers can take some satisfaction from all
three statements. However, the observation I wanted to make dealt with the example I used previously of the difficulty a dairy farmer has here in Canada compared to one south of the State of Georgia, particularly in Florida. I also wonder if the Hon. Member knows that the U.S. dairy industry can send ice cream across the bridge from, say Detroit but we do not have access to the U.S. market. That concerns me. It might well be an interesting item to raise, but we will not be raising it unless we are requested to do so by the industry.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Resuming debate with the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon).

Mr. Speaker, let me start off by saying that my sympathies lie with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) as he tries desperately to defend his farmers, as he sees them, against the assault posed by the free trade agreement. He is, as I see it, agonizing his way along as toughly as he can. Frankly, I wish him luck, but I also have to say that I think farmers across the country will find some very rude surprises in what is going to take place.
That is your wish.
That is not my wish.
Indeed it is.
That is not my wish. I have dairy farmers in my riding.
Not many of them. How many?

Far fewer than there used to be, and that is a commentary on past agricultural policy. However, those who are there are very concerned about what may happen not just because of the potential threat to the dairy industry, but also because of the potential threat to cross-boundary product movements which could undercut the industry and in turn undercut farmers and the farm sector itself. I wanted to make that point at the beginning.
This is perhaps one of the most important debates which has taken place on the economic future of this country since 1867. We have to choose the direction we are going to take, and that has tremendous implications for our future as a sovereign nation. There is, too, a broader issue involved in this debate. That issue is crucial to all Canadians. That is, the question of the integrity of Ministers who now stand behind this policy when they stood behind quite a different policy prior to their election. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) started this debate with some quotations and I want to do the same. I would like to begin with a quotation from the Secretary of State concerning free trade with the U.S. This is from Maclean's in 1983: "It is silly. Canada must improve relations and trade with the United States, of course, but our natural destiny is to become a global leader, not America's weak sister." Let me quote as well the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) from the same source: "Bilateral free trade with the U.S. is simplistic and naive. It would only serve further to
March 16, 1987

diminish our ability to compete internationally." Either the Minister did not believe it then or he is agonizing over supporting what is taking place now. Finally, let me quote the Prime Minister from that same source: "Canadians rejected free trade with the U.S. in 1911. They would do so again in 1983. Canada must increase its share of total world trade which has dropped by 33 per cent in the past two decades."
What we have here is a series of leading economic Ministers who, when they were seeking the leadership of the Conservative Party, and I could quote the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) if I wanted to on this issue, indicated very clearly that they were against free trade. Yet once elected with this vast majority, they led the country in the direction of a comprehensive agreement with the U.S. That carries some extreme dangers, not just for our future sovereignty but for our economic well-being. Those remarks apply to what the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) said today. She made the most remarkable statements about the Auto Pact being an example of free trade and how she wished all the country could share in it. Those of us in southern Ontario who benefited from the Auto Pact and therefore from free trade should be willing to share our goodies. Let me make it quite clear that if the Minister still believes that an agreement which has safeguards both with respect to numbers of cars which must be produced in this country and with respect to Canadian content is in fact free trade, then she simply does not understand anything about the definition of the portfolio in which she is required to work.
I must take this point further. In his remarkable speech this morning, which in so many words said so little, the Prime Minister came at one point to a rather remarkable conclusion. He said,that every research study had shown that there would be tremendous economic benefits for this country. I have here on my desk enough research reports which have shown exactly the contrary to keep this House busy for hours. I have one from the University of Maryland which says that among 28 industrial sectors analysed in this report the net employment is positive in 5 industrial sectors and negative in the remaining 23 sectors.
I can quote as well from reports of the Government of Ontario undertaken by Jack Baranson, an American who is unlikely to be biased on this. He makes the point very forcefully in that research report that there will be a tremendous outpouring of American branch plants from this country.
I can make the point with respect to studies done by the Province of Quebec which indicated significant job losses which would take place in Quebec. I can make the point with respect to another study done for the Government with respect to the Auto Pact and its conclusions which said that the Auto Pact should not be permitted in any way to be affected by this negotiation. It is quite clear now that it will be affected by this negotiation if across-the-board tariff cuts are going to be put into place.
Bilateral Trade
Abundant research reports have demonstrated that the Prime Minister's points to us this morning and to the nation were not, as they should have been, reflections of reality but instead were reflections of hope. If he actually read the research reports which have been done on this subject by a great many groups across the country which include sectoral studies which have finally been produced, not by the Government publicly, but by the-

Quebec Coalition against free trade, groups which commissioned those studies carried out by Quebec economists, which clearly stated that in all the industries which were considered, there will be terrible losses as a result of that free trade arrangement.

That is in fact what the studies have shown us and that is in fact what the Prime Minister should be aware of as he speaks to this House and the nation.
He also spoke this morning about the resolution which came out of the New Democratic Party's convention over the past weekend. In that, too, he was selective. He chose the one point which he wished to attack without making clear to the nation that in that resolution was a very broad and detailed trade strategy that would take us in a different direction which would give us trade expansion with the rest of the world including the United States but would not sell us out as the present trade initiative is clearly going to do.
I could talk about some of those alternatives. I could talk, for instance, about the support for small business and mediumsized firms which the Government has not been prepared to give in the export sector through the EDC as it should have. I could talk about the necessity of working to build up more production and import replacement in high-tech sectors in this country through planning with business and labour. I could talk about an extension of the approach that has been taken in the Auto Pact and its 60 per cent Canadian content rules which would give us thousands of new jobs right across the country. I could also talk about the realities as opposed to the myths of GATT presented by both the Minister for International Trade and the Prime Minister.
The reality is that GATT is urgently trying to deal with many of the problems which we are being hit by from the United States; the problems we have seen in softwood lumber, the problems we have seen in fish, and the problems we experience in Ontario in pork. That is a route which can be taken which would give us rapid action toward solving the problems that face us.
I could talk, as well, about the need to establish dispute settlement mechanisms which I think would be quite helpful between ourselves and the United States. That is the kind of strategy which can and should be taken in this country. However, that is not the direction which is being taken and across the country, contrary to the quotations which the Prime Minister read this morning. There is a crescendo of opposition

March 16, 1987
Business of the House
emerging to this free trade thrust, opposition which I am predicting will lead to this thrust being rejected in the end despite the brave words of the Prime Minister this morning.
I could quote from the Gazette of March 14 which suggests that the Government should clarify its position on Monday because it has not clarified it yet. I could quote from Won-nacott's, economists who have supported free trade in many respects and who say that because a free trade arrangement is bound to create a number of specific problems it would best be undertaken when major disturbances such as widespread unemployment or an international financial crisis are absent. That, as we all know, represents the conditions which face us at this stage in Canada with 9.6 per cent out of work.
I could quote from Albert Breton, a member of the Macdonald Commission, who says:
I continue to hold that anti-Americanism in Canada can be better kept in check and the prospect for free trade over the long term better protected, if unilateral reinterpretation of fair trade laws by the U.S. Government is directed at all its trading partners, rather than if a bilateral agreement calls "special" attention to Canada.
As Breton says, what will stop the U.S. Government from unilaterally reinterpreting and redefining any agreements, however formal, between Ottawa and Washington? Certainly not a sense of fairness or responsibility or even respect for the written word. I could quote from Arthur Donner who states:
All of this suggests that Canada should not count on a free trade pact with the U.S. to rescue it from its productivity doldrums. Aside from the politics of the issue, Ottawa should be looking at other ways of boosting the economy and productivity.
I could quote Peter Francis, a small boat manufacturer who owns ACF Grew Inc., who states:
If free trade becomes a reality, I expect to see some U.S. companies retreat across the border and serve the Canadian market from their larger and more efficient plants. I would not be at all surprised if we find Canadian companies establishing their new plants in the U.S. sun belt, where unions are practically nonexistent and a large number of employees work for minimum wages and benefits.
I could quote the head of Labatt's, who says:
The costs of free trade are very high. Under present conditions, any economic advantages of free trade to the American brewing industry would be offset by severe financial and human dislocation in the Canadian brewing industry.
Perhaps I could finish by quoting George Grant, who has been a member and supporter of the Conservative Party for many years. He says:
There seems to be no doubt that Canadian political sovereignty would be put in question both domestically and internationally if our two societies were homogenized economically. For example, social security policies: we just could not have policies that put us at a taxation disadvantage.
That is the reality that faces us if this path is taken. There is another path by which this country can get back on its feet.
This Parliament must address itself to those dreams of our children and communities throughout the country of a free, independent sovereign nation which will be able to direct its own affairs so that it will not be told, as in the case of softwood lumber, what it can and cannot do. We must look toward a sovereign future in which Washington does not tell us what we can and cannot do in a free trade agreement. We must direct what takes place and decide how we shape our regional development policies, our agricultural strategies, our cultural policies and our development.
That is not the direction in which the Government is taking us. Rather, we are faced with camouflage by the Government and must rely on information that leaks from the chief negotiator and Canadian press in order to get a sense of what is on the negotiating table.
If the Government wanted to regain its sense of leadership on this issue, today was its opportunity to do so by giving the House a real progress report instead of a bogus set of presentations that have not explained what is taking place in the free trade talks.
We want the dream of the future, we do not want bogus directions which will be so devastating for all of us in the future.
